findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report V1
findings.headline: Local unemployment has risen 54% year-on-year to 5.1%, above regional average of 4%
findings.detail: Unemployment reached 5.1% in Q3 2025/26, up from 4.2% in Q2 2025/26 and 3.3% in Q3 2024/25. This 54% year-on-year increase significantly exceeds the Yorkshire and Humber regional average of 4% and indicates local labour market deterioration.
findings.matters: Rising local unemployment cascades into multiple council financial pressures: reduced business rates, increased welfare demand, housing arrears (already rising 3.59%), homelessness pressure, and potential council tax collection risk. It is a leading indicator of worsening fiscal stress.
findings.quote: Unemployment Rate: Performance 5.1% (11,300 / 221,569) (Q3 2025/26) - Worse than Q2 2025/26 (by 0.9 pp) - Worse than Q3 2024/25 (by 1.8 pp)

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report V1
findings.headline: Children in Need caseload surged 26% year-on-year: 570 additional cases in Q1 2026/27
findings.detail: Children in Need reached 2,735 in Q1 2026/27, up 570 (26%) from Q1 2025/26 and 347 (14.6%) from Q4 2025/26. This statutory safeguarding metric shows strong upward trend with no explanation provided for drivers of demand growth.
findings.matters: Children in Need is a leading indicator for children's social care cost growth and escalation to child protection. A 26% year-on-year increase in a service already flagged as having structural cost pressures will translate into higher assessment, plan, and support service costs.
findings.figures: 2,735 children in need (up 570 year-on-year, 26% growth; up 347 quarterly, 14.6% growth)
findings.quote: Number of Children in Need: 2,735 (Q1 2026/27) - Increase on Q4 2025/26 (by 347 children) - Increase on Q1 2025/26 (by 570 children)

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report V1
findings.headline: Housing Register demand growing sharply: 1,554 more applicants year-on-year (7.5% growth)
findings.detail: Housing Register applicants reached 22,209 in Q1 2026/27, up 1,554 from Q1 2025/26 and up 320 from Q4 2025/26. This rapid growth signals increased housing stress and will drive future demand for temporary accommodation, affordable housing delivery, and housing management resources.
findings.matters: Rapid housing register growth indicates growing housing insecurity in the population. This directly drives temporary accommodation spending, capital commitments for affordable housing, and creates potential future homelessness pressure. It correlates with rising unemployment and tenant arrears.
findings.figures: 22,209 applicants Q1 2026/27 (up 1,554 from Q1 2025/26; 7.5% annual growth)
findings.quote: Number of applicants on Housing Register: 22,209 (Q1 2026/27) - Increase on Q4 2025/26 (by 320 applications) - Increase on Q1 2025/26 (by 1,554 applications)

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report V1
findings.headline: Tenant arrears rising: 3.59% of rent due, up from 3.38% a year ago
findings.detail: Housing rent arrears reached 3.59% (£3.79m of £105.6m due) in Q1 2026/27, up from 3.38% in Q1 2025/26. This deterioration is occurring despite reported positive trends in direct debit uptake and proactive arrears management. The rise correlates with unemployment increasing to 5.1% (up from 3.3% year-on-year).
findings.matters: Rising tenant arrears are a leading indicator of household financial stress. Combined with 54% unemployment increase in the same period, this signals genuine economic stress in the tenant population that will worsen further if economic conditions deteriorate.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report V1
findings.headline: Home to school transport costs rising: 4% annual demand growth alongside deteriorating contract market
findings.detail: Home to school transport pupil numbers grew 4% (63 pupils) comparing Q1 2025/26 to Q1 2026/27, reflecting ongoing SEND population growth. The service faces 'challenging market conditions for private contracts' which means 'the service is continuing to see increased costs' despite ongoing efficiency improvements and use of in-house provision.
findings.matters: This is a statutory, demand-driven service with rigid entitlements. Combining 4% annual pupil growth with deteriorating contract market creates structural cost inflation that cannot be controlled through efficiency. A lender would see this as uncontrollable recurring spending.
findings.figures: 4% increase (63 pupils) Q1 2025/26 to Q1 2026/27; ongoing upward trend in SEND population
findings.quote: Comparing Quarter 1 of 2025/6 to Quarter 1 of 2026/7 shows an increase overall of 63 pupils or a 4% increase in numbers accessing the service... challenging market conditions for private contracts, means the service is continuing to see increased costs.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report V1
findings.headline: EHCP processing has collapsed: only 17.27% issued within 20-week statutory target, down from 58.7% a year ago
findings.detail: Only 19 of 110 EHCPs (17.27%) were issued within the 20-week statutory expectation in Q1 2026/27, with average time now 22 weeks. This represents a 71% drop in compliance from Q1 2025/26 (58.7%). Capacity is under pressure across educational psychologists, social care, and therapists. EHCP demand has grown to 5,171 plans (up 303 year-on-year).
findings.matters: This is a statutory service with legal penalties for non-compliance. Systematic failure to meet timelines triggers tribunals, legal challenge costs, and reputational damage. Growing demand combined with capacity constraints will force unbudgeted spending on locum staff and tribunal defence.
findings.figures: 17.27% (19/110) Q1 2026/27 vs 58.7% Q1 2025/26; average issuance 22 weeks; 5,171 EHCPs (up 303 year-on-year)
findings.quote: The average time for issuing plans is around 22 weeks. Issuing plans requires advice to be provided by a range of professionals, including Educational Psychologists, Social Care, Speech and Language Therapists and Occupational Therapists. Capacity across all these areas is under pressure.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report V1
findings.headline: Significant underlying cost pressures in adults and children's social care remain persistent despite reserves improving
findings.detail: The council reported usable reserves increased by £1.4m at end of 2025/26, but this masks significant underlying cost pressures in adults and children's social care causing 'concern from a medium-term financial sustainability viewpoint.' These pressures remain at similar levels in Q1 2026/27. The MTFS being prepared for October Cabinet must reflect these issues, and services are being asked to reduce pressures in-year.
findings.matters: Structural cost deficits in the largest council services cannot be resolved through reserves. A lender would see persistent underlying pressures as indicating either demand-driven inflation or service model dysfunction that requires fundamental transformation, not temporary budget fixes.
findings.figures: £1.4m reserves increase, but underlying cost pressures flagged as persistent in Q1 2026/27
findings.quote: However as reported in the outturn there were significant underlying cost pressures within adults and children's social care which were causing concern from a medium-term financial sustainability viewpoint. It is apparent from Q1 that these cost pressures remain to a very similar extent.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A 25-26 HN Annual Complaints Performance Service Improvement Report
findings.headline: Damp and mould service moved from 'peak backlog conditions' to business-as-usual by June 2025, revealing prior operational stress
findings.detail: Between January and June 2025, a significant operational backlog in damp, mould and condensation handling was resolved through co-location of teams into a single integrated service. This rapid shift from peak backlog to steady state indicates the service had been under acute strain. Damp/mould remains a leading complaint driver (12% of all complaints) with multiple Housing Ombudsman determinations. Awaab's Law compliance is cited as a driver for ongoing focus.
findings.matters: Backlogs in regulated services indicate stretched capacity or process failure; the six-month backlog recovery suggests either sudden spike in demand or prior underinvestment; damp/mould has regulatory compliance implications
findings.figures: Damp/mould 12% of all new complaints; multiple maladministration findings on this category; backlog cleared within six months of January 2025 intervention
findings.quote: Between January and June 2025, the Council moved from peak backlog conditions to a business‑as‑usual position. All relevant team were co‑located creating a single, integrated service responsible for managing cases of damp, mould and condensation from the residents initial report through survey, treatment, repairs and aftercare, improving visibility, accountability and data accuracy.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A 25-26 HN Annual Complaints Performance Service Improvement Report
findings.headline: Cabinet committed £390m five-year Housing Capital Investment Plan in December 2025, but core complaint volumes remain unchanged
findings.detail: The plan aims to reduce property-condition complaints through planned capital works and improved maintenance. However, Stage 1 complaint rates remain at 37.29 per 1,000 homes (essentially unchanged from 36.54 last year), and repair/property condition complaints remain the largest category at 46% of all complaints. The Stock Condition Survey is being accelerated to inform investment. An independent management review is due 30 June 2026.
findings.matters: A large capital commitment requires demonstrable ROI and effective delivery; the absence of early improvement in key metrics raises questions about whether management can execute the plan and whether root causes are correctly understood
findings.figures: £390m commitment over 5 years; Stage 1 complaints 37.29 per 1,000 homes (vs 36.54 prior year); 46% of new complaints concern property condition/repairs; damp/mould 12%
findings.quote: Cabinet approved a £390m five-year Housing Capital Investment Plan in December 2025, setting out how the council will continue to invest in and improve its housing stock. The plan provides a long-term commitment to ensuring homes are safe, decent and fit for the future, while meeting regulatory requirements and supporting service improvements. This is expected to support a reduction in complaints relating to property condition and repairs.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A 25-26 HN Annual Complaints Performance Service Improvement Report
findings.headline: Housing Ombudsman found maladministration or service failure in 69% of cases, a worsening trend
findings.detail: Of 67 determinations issued between April 2025 and March 2026, approximately 69% identified failings — described as 'a slight increase on the previous year.' Recurring themes include damp/mould mishandling, anti-social behaviour delays, repair failures, and complaint handling breakdowns. The council has commissioned an independent review of its complaints handling due 30 June 2026.
findings.matters: A high and worsening rate of regulatory maladministration findings in a compliance-sensitive service indicates systemic control weaknesses or capacity constraints that could affect other services and expose the council to reputational or enforcement risk
findings.figures: 69% of 67 outcomes; 46% of complaints about property condition/repair; 12% damp/mould; 11.5% anti-social behaviour; multiple Ombudsman orders for compensation, apologies, staff training and inspections
findings.quote: During the period April 2025 to March 2026, the Ombudsman issued 67 outcomes, with approximately 69% identifying failings across our services. This is a slight increase on the previous year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A 25-26 HN Annual Complaints Performance Service Improvement Report
findings.headline: Tenant satisfaction with complaints handling is 25%, more than 10 points below the 36.1% benchmark
findings.detail: Only 25% of residents who made complaints reported satisfaction with the council's handling, versus a benchmark of 36.1%. Speed satisfaction was 40%, information satisfaction 43%, and process-ease satisfaction 46%, all below what benchmarks indicate is achievable elsewhere.
findings.matters: Service quality this far below peer benchmarks signals management or process problems; satisfaction levels influence tenant confidence and behaviour, affecting collections and voids
findings.figures: Satisfaction: 25% vs 36.1% benchmark (11-point gap); n=1,775 tenants surveyed (8% of households)
findings.quote: Of the surveys responded to, 27% of respondents said they were happy with the overall handling of their complaint, 46% found the process easy, 40% were happy with speed of the complaint handling, 68% said they would be comfortable to make a complaint in the future and 43% were happy with the information provided throughout their complaint.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A 25-26 HN Annual Complaints Performance Service Improvement Report
findings.headline: Stage 1 complaint handling compliance declined sharply to 71.54%, well below the 96.3% benchmark
findings.detail: The council responded to Stage 1 complaints within required timescales (10 working days) in only 71.54% of cases in 2025/26, down from 82.71% the prior year. This represents deteriorating performance in a regulated service, against a benchmark of 96.3%. The council acknowledges this requires improvement.
findings.matters: Declining compliance in complaint handling — a core regulated function — suggests operational or capacity strain; the gap to benchmark indicates systematic underperformance relative to peers
findings.figures: 71.54% (2025–26) vs 82.71% (2024–25); benchmark 96.3%; service-wide target miss of ~25 percentage points
findings.quote: At Stage 1 of the complaints process we handled 69.20% of complaints within the timescales set out in the code i.e. 5 working days to log, define and acknowledge the complaint and provide a response within 10 working days. This is very similar to last year and against a target of 96.3%. However, we recognise this is an area of our performance that requires improvement.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Cover Report - Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report
findings.headline: Subject Access Request compliance collapsed to 49% due to staffing vacancies and rising demand
findings.detail: SAR response times fell to 49% compliance (down 16 percentage points from prior year) and FOI compliance fell to 75% (down 2%). Root causes identified as rising demand, backlogs, and staffing vacancies. Recruitment is underway and improved monitoring tools are being developed.
findings.matters: Persistent compliance failures on data requests expose the council to legal risk and indicate operational stress and capability constraints.
findings.figures: SAR compliance 49% (down 16 pp); FOI compliance 75% (down 2 pp); 565 FOI requests received vs 449 prior year; 188 SARs vs 133 prior year
findings.quote: Compliance within expected timescales for responding fell to 75% for FOIs down by 2% compared to Q1 2025/26 and 49% for SARs down by 16% compared to Q1 2025/26, mainly due to rising demand, backlogs and staffing vacancies

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Cover Report - Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report
findings.headline: Employment rate declined to 72.7% as economic inactivity rises, threatening future tax base
findings.detail: Employment rate fell from 74.9% in Q2 2025-26 to 72.7% in Q3 2025-26, driven by increasing economic inactivity and reduced recruitment opportunities. Council is focusing on employer engagement and support for economically inactive residents.
findings.matters: Falling employment erodes the council tax collection base and typically increases demand for council support services.
findings.figures: Employment rate 72.7% (Q3 2025-26) vs 74.9% (Q2 2025-26); 2.2 percentage point decline
findings.quote: the employment rate at 72.7% at Q3 2025/26 compared to 74.9% at Q2 2025/26, due to increasing economic inactivity and reduced recruitment opportunities

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Cover Report - Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report
findings.headline: Housing rent arrears increased to 3.59%, above prior-year level
findings.detail: Council housing rent arrears rose to 3.59% in Q1 2026-27, described as slightly higher than the previous year. This represents erosion of rental income.
findings.matters: Rising arrears indicate growing payment difficulties among tenants and reduce actual housing revenue available to the council.
findings.quote: Rent arrears stood at 3.59%, slightly higher than the previous year

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Cover Report - Q1 2026-27 Council Plan and Performance Update Report
findings.headline: Home to School Transport demand for SEND pupils growing faster than inflation, driving multi-year efficiency programme
findings.detail: Transport support for children with Special Educational Needs reached 1,586 in Q1 2026-27, up 63 from the same quarter last year (1,523), reflecting continuing long-term growth. The council acknowledges this trend and is undertaking a multi-year transformation programme focused on managing efficiency and value for money.
findings.matters: Sustained growth in high-need transport services drives revenue pressures; the need for transformation suggests current cost trajectory is unsustainable.
findings.figures: 1,586 children in Q1 2026-27; 63 more than Q1 2025-26 (1,523); continuing long-term growth trend
findings.quote: Demand for Home to School Transport remains high, driven by increasing numbers of children with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) and EHCPs. At the end of Q1 2026/27, 1,586 children were receiving transport support... 63 more than Q1 2025/26 with 1,523, reflecting the continuing long-term growth trend.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Community Asset Transfer Policy 2020
findings.headline: Assets are transferred below market value, meaning the council does not capture full capital value
findings.detail: The policy states assets are transferred below market value for social or community benefit. This is a deliberate choice by the council to forego market-value capital receipts that could be realized through sale, reducing available capital funding.
findings.matters: The council is explicitly not maximizing capital receipts from asset disposals, which affects available funding for investment or debt reduction
findings.figures: No valuations provided in policy
findings.quote: Assets are transferred at less than market value for local social, economic or environmental benefit.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Community Asset Transfer Policy 2020
findings.headline: Council commits to ongoing annual revenue grants of 15% in year 1 and 5% in year 2 for each transferred asset
findings.detail: Following completion of each transfer, the council will pay revenue grants to the community organization managing the asset, calculated as percentages of that asset's previous operational running costs (excluding staffing). With 21 successful transfers already completed as of August 2020, these are direct ongoing financial commitments that reduce council revenue available for other services.
findings.matters: Each CAT creates a multi-year financial liability on the council's revenue budget that compounds as more transfers occur
findings.figures: 15% of average running cost year 1; 5% year 2; 21 successful transfers as of August 2020
findings.quote: A grant equivalent to 15% of the average running cost will be paid on completion of the transfer and a further grant equivalent to 5% the following year.

findings.headline: Unallocated reserves at £27m minimum; headroom above £22m minimum working balance is only £5m
findings.detail: The council holds total useable reserves of £75m (unallocated £27m, earmarked £48m). The unallocated reserves are only £5m above the stated £22m minimum working balance, leaving minimal buffer. The council is drawing down earmarked reserves (forecast £1.852m net drawdown in Q1) to support current spending. At this rate, unallocated reserves provide limited protection.
findings.matters: Thin unallocated reserves leave the council vulnerable to any further adverse variance and limit capacity to absorb external shocks
findings.figures: £27m unallocated reserves vs £22m minimum working balance (£5m headroom), £48m earmarked reserves, forecast £1.852m net drawdown in Q1
findings.quote: Total Useable Reserves of £75m* at 31st March 2027 of which: Unallocated reserves of £27m / Earmarked Reserves of £48m

findings.headline: Court cost fee recovery shortfall building; council tax collection fee rules changing
findings.detail: The Welfare and Exchequer budget shows a £157k court cost fee recovery shortfall. The paper notes this is "likely to worsen due to proposed changes in Council tax rules on collecting outstanding debt and capped fees" and that pressure on court cost recovery has been built into the MTFS from 2027/28 onward.
findings.matters: Declining income from court costs signals both reduced debt enforcement (collection problems) and regulatory caps limiting recovery; a trend that will worsen
findings.figures: £157k court cost fee recovery shortfall
findings.quote: Court Cost Fee Recovery shortfall and likely to worsen due to proposed changes in Council tax rules on collecting outstanding debt and capped fees

findings.headline: Housing benefit subsidy loss £570k; bed and breakfast accommodation costs unrecoverable
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £570k overspend on housing benefit subsidy due to bed and breakfast and nightly-paid temporary accommodation costs that are not fully recoverable under Housing Benefit subsidy rules. The mitigation actions note ongoing investigations into moving Ashenhurst to HRA and assessment of alternative temporary accommodation models.
findings.matters: A structural mismatch between temporary accommodation spend and subsidy recovery that requires model change to resolve; indicates growing rough sleeping or homelessness demand
findings.figures: £570k overspend on Housing Benefit subsidy
findings.quote: Cost of bed and breakfast and other nightly paid temporary accommodation not fully recoverable through the Housing Benefit subsidy rules

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to rise to £1,068m; debt rising and financing costs increasing to 9.6% of revenue stream
findings.detail: The CFR is forecast to grow from £987.2m (2025/26 actual) to £1,068.3m (2026/27 forecast) to £1,191m (2027/28 budget). Financing costs are rising: General Fund financing costs are £46.8m in 2026/27 (9.6% of net revenue stream), rising to £59.8m by 2028/29 (10.4%). The council is relying heavily on prudential borrowing (£98.5m new borrowing in capital plan) to fund £287m capital expenditure.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs consume an increasing share of revenue budget, crowding out service spending and leaving less headroom for pressures
findings.quote: General Fund - Financing costs (£m) 46.8. General Fund – Proportion of net revenue stream 9.6%

findings.headline: School transport overspending £867k; passenger assistant and taxi costs rising
findings.detail: School transport is forecast £867k over budget due to overspends on passenger assistant staffing (£340k on hired staff) and pre-16 taxi and personal travel budget costs (£330k taxi overspend, £136k PTB). The council attributes this to staffing shortages and increased use of external transport providers.
findings.matters: Rising transport costs, driven by reliance on agency staff and external suppliers, is an easily controllable but recurring overspend
findings.figures: £867k total overspend, £340k overspend on hired passenger assistants, £330k overspend on taxis, £136k on personal travel budgets
findings.quote: Overspend on Employees – Passenger Assistants, substantive staffing forecasts to break-even (fully staffed) plus over-spend on use of Hired Staff (£340k). Over-spend on Pre-16 Transport: Taxis (£330k), Personal Travel Budgets (£136k)

findings.headline: Adults social care placement costs £3.4m overspent on older people home care; 48 more people in placements than budgeted
findings.detail: Older people physical disability home care is forecast £3.4m over budget. Residential and nursing placements show 48 more people in care than the budget assumed, with nursing costs £165 per week over budget. Learning disabilities residential and nursing placements are also overspent (£3.019m on mental health alone, with 25 more people than budgeted). These are demand pressures driving recurring overspends.
findings.matters: Adult social care demand is rising faster than budgeted and costs are exceeding assumed unit rates; this is a structural problem that will repeat next year
findings.figures: £3.4m overspend on PD home care, 48 more OP placements than budget, nursing cost £165 per week over budget; MH residential 25 more placements, cost £219 per week over budget, £3.019m overspend
findings.quote: Despite a forecast reduction to the number of people expected in Self Directed Support and Home Care, the cost of PD home care is currently forecast to be £3.4m over budget

findings.headline: Children's external residential placements £6.7m overspent; 53 placements vs 35 budgeted
findings.detail: The council budgeted for 35 external residential placements for children but now forecasts 53 active placements. The average cost per week is £7,183 vs £6,273 budgeted, creating a £6.735m variance. External fostering adds another £2.330m overspend (199 placements vs 180 budgeted). These are demand-driven costs with no evident containment plan.
findings.matters: The council has lost control of placement costs and volumes; these are entitlements that cannot easily be reduced, threatening future-year budgets
findings.figures: £6.735m overspend on external residential (53 placements vs 35 budgeted), average cost £7,183 vs £6,273 budgeted per week; £2.330m overspend on external fostering
findings.quote: £6,735k external residential. Higher cost and volume (Average cost £7,183 vs £6,273 per week. Placements at 53 vs 35 budgeted)

findings.headline: DSG cumulative deficit projected to reach £110m by March 2027; in-year deficit £28.7m
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant is funding a £28.7m in-year deficit. The cumulative deficit opens at £81.3m and is forecast to close at £110m before payment of historic deficits. The primary driver is independent school placements: 267 places forecast at an average cost of £65k (up from 254 placements at £58.3k cost in 2025/26), consuming £17.3m. The council has no solution to this embedded problem.
findings.matters: An uncapped statutory liability that grows each year and cannot be carried forward indefinitely without triggering council instability; eventually requires top-up from general fund or a debt write-off
findings.figures: £28.7m in-year deficit, £81.3m opening cumulative deficit, £110m projected closing deficit, 267 independent placements at £65k average (£17.3m total)
findings.quote: Independent School Place numbers and costs continue to increase. 25/26 Outturn position was 254 placements, cost £14.8m – this is now increased to 267 places, forecasted cost of £17.3m. Average cost per placement is now £65k (was £58.3k at end of 2025-26)

findings.headline: Budget savings target 63% delivered; £8m shortfall against £21.8m total target
findings.detail: The council has only achieved 63% of its total savings target, with an £8m shortfall against £21.8m target. The 2026/27 savings target of £10.5m is tracking £2.5m short. Previously agreed savings from 2025/26 of £10.3m are projected to shortfall by £5.5m. This means planned reductions to services are not being implemented as forecast.
findings.matters: If savings targets are being missed this early in the year, recovery is unlikely; this signals either poor planning or inability to deliver cuts, forcing ongoing reserve reliance
findings.figures: £8m shortfall against £21.8m total target (63% delivery), 2026/27 target £10.5m projected shortfall £2.5m, previously agreed £10.3m projected shortfall £5.5m
findings.quote: Budget savings shortfall - £8m against total target of £21.8m. (63% delivery)

findings.headline: £13.6m projected General Fund overspend after drawing £5.2m from reserves
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £13.6m overspend after drawing down £5.2m from budget reserves. The General Fund variance shows £18.85m forecast overspend before reserve use. Key pressure areas are Children and Families (£8.255m), Adults and Health (£10.749m), and Place (£1.8m), partially offset by Public Health & Corporate Resources (£953k underspend) and Central Budgets (£1.001m underspend).
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can balance its budget without emergency reserve draws and how long reserves can sustain current spending levels
findings.figures: £13.6m projected overspend, £5.2m budget reserve drawdown, £18.85m General Fund variance pre-reserves, £75m total useable reserves (unallocated £27m)
findings.quote: Projected overspend of £13.6m after use of £5.2m budget reserve

findings.headline: Data Processing/GDPR: Subject Access Request backlog and processing time non-compliance; ICO monitoring closely
findings.detail: LGC02 (amber, 15) notes risk of regulatory censure and fines due to backlog of Subject Access Requests (SARs) and linked SARs processing time performance. SARs rose 24% during 2025-26; Q1 reporting suggests numbers may drop across 2026-27 but current compliance rates are at risk. ICO recognises challenges and is monitoring situation closely; failure to resolve satisfactorily may result in formal reprimand or other ICO action.
findings.matters: Active ICO monitoring indicates regulatory attention; non-compliance could result in formal action and reputational damage; suggests data governance capacity issues.
findings.figures: SARs rose 24% in 2025-26; ICO monitoring compliance closely
findings.quote: Risk score is maintained due to the backlog of Subject Access Requests (SARs) and linked SARs processing time performance. The ICO recognise the challenges that we face and are monitoring the situation closely. Failure to resolve satisfactorily may result in formal reprimand or other ICO action. SARs rose by 24% during 2025-26 compared with the previous year with an anticipated impact on compliance rates.

findings.headline: Adults Safeguarding risk escalated: sustained increase in Safeguarding Adult Review volume may indicate systemic weakness
findings.detail: AH01 increased from 8 to 12 (amber). Sustained increases in volume of Safeguarding Adults Reviews raised at the Safeguarding Adults Board "may indicate a higher risk safeguarding environment, pressure on partnership arrangements and service capacity with potential system wide weaknesses". Resourcing implications have been flagged at board level.
findings.matters: Rising SAR volume may signal failures in upstream prevention and risk management; resourcing implications suggest cost pressure and potential regulatory/reputational risk.
findings.figures: AH01 score increased from 8 to 12; sustained increase in SAR volumes (specific number not stated)
findings.quote: Sustained increases to the volume of Safeguarding Adults Review (SAR) raised at KSAB may indicate a higher risk safeguarding environment, pressure on partnership arrangements and service capacity with potential system wide weaknesses. Resourcing implications of increasing volumes has been raised at KSAB.

findings.headline: Unison strike action ballot over 2026 pay award rejection; Kirklees identified as targeted authority
findings.detail: PS02 risk score increased due to complexity of employee relations cases and tribunal delays. The 2026 pay award has been rejected and unions are balloting for strike action over the summer. Kirklees is specifically named as one of Unison's targeted local authorities. Staff handbook review underway with potential to cause further union disquiet. New Employment Rights Act also creating implementation demands.
findings.matters: Strike action would disrupt service delivery across council operations; identified as targeted authority by major union signals elevated risk of action.
findings.figures: PS02 score increased from prior quarter; Unison ballot underway summer 2026
findings.quote: Score has increased this quarter reflecting the volume and complexity of employee relations matters which are being further impacted by delays with tribunal cases. The 2026 pay award has been rejected and unions are balloting for strike action over the summer. Kirklees is one of Unison's targeted local authorities.

findings.headline: Supreme Court judgment on Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) from June 2 June 2026 changes legal framework with immediate effect
findings.detail: AH03 is new to Corporate Risk Report (amber, 12). 2 June 2026 Supreme Court ruling changed the legal framework underpinning DoLS and DoLICS "with immediate effect". Previous 2014 Cheshire West judgment provided clear threshold; loss of this creates "increased risk of inconsistency and variation in interpretations" with impacts across frontline practice, commissioned provision, and operations. Legal review, process changes, and training underway; potential liability implications.
findings.matters: Introduces legal compliance risk and potential liability exposure; changes in operational requirements and workload capacity not yet fully quantified.
findings.figures: AH03 new risk scored 12 (amber); judgment effective 2 June 2026
findings.quote: On 2 June 2026, the UK Supreme Court handed down a judgement which changes the legal framework underpinning DoLS and DoLICS within Adult Social Care, with immediate effect. The previous 2014 Cheshire West judgement provided a clear and consistent threshold for identifying when legal safeguards were required, without this there is increased risk of inconsistency and variation in interpretations. The change in legal interpretation and application has impacts across frontline practice, commissioned provision, operational processes and system recording.

findings.headline: SEND Safety Valve Agreement ended; council must now fund 10% of historic DSG deficit from own resources
findings.detail: The Safety Valve Agreement has ended. Central government will pay 90% of historic (pre-March 2026) DSG deficits, but the council must fund the remaining 10% contribution. This is a new unfunded liability with no specified solution date. Additionally, cost and numbers of independent school placements continue to exceed budget lines in the High Needs Block.
findings.matters: Removes central government protection on a substantial historic deficit; creates a new, permanent revenue liability and signals ongoing structural pressure in SEND spend.
findings.figures: 10% council contribution to historic DSG deficit (pre-March 2026); independent school placement costs exceed budget lines
findings.quote: The SEND Safety Valve Agreement has ended. Central government will pay 90% of the historic (pre-March 2026) DSG deficits and a plan will be required to fund the remaining 10% contribution. Cost, and numbers of independent school placements continue to exceed budget lines in the High Needs Block.

findings.headline: Budget overspends in Adults and Children's Services in Q1 2026/27, with savings targets missed in 2025/26
findings.detail: FIN01 escalated to red (16) from amber. Q1 shows overspends in both Adults and Children's Services. Additional 2026/27 funding may be insufficient to mitigate volatility in social care demand. The document notes that "2025-26 savings initiatives did not deliver in line with forecast and therefore the agreed savings targets were not achieved", with most rolled forward to 2026/27.
findings.matters: In-year overspends in Q1 signal immediate budget pressure and failure to deliver planned savings undermines medium-term planning credibility.
findings.figures: FIN01 risk score increased to 16 (from 12); risk escalated from amber to red
findings.quote: There are increasing delivery risks to the agreed 2026-27 budget, as seen by the budget overspends within both Adults and Children's Services at the end of Q1 2026-27. Additional funding in 2026-27 budgets to manage cost pressures may be insufficient to fully mitigate with continued volatility across social care demand budgets. 2025-26 savings initiatives did not deliver in line with forecast and therefore the agreed savings targets were not achieved.

findings.headline: Budget contingency reserve will be exhausted in-year and further earmarked reserves will need to be used, indicating depletion of financial resilience
findings.detail: The strategic budget contingency reserve of £5.2m will be fully used to offset the Q1 overspend. The paper notes that further drawdowns from other earmarked reserves will be needed to balance the budget, though the full impact has not yet been quantified. Any use of reserves must be replenished in 2027/28, which will reduce the council's flexibility to deal with future shocks or pressures. This cycle of reserve depletion and replenishment is unsustainable.
findings.matters: Depletion of contingency reserves indicates the council is losing financial resilience. The need to replenish reserves in 2027/28 will absorb significant resources that might otherwise be available for services or to address budget pressures, creating a vicious cycle.
findings.figures: Strategic budget contingency reserve £5.2m (to be fully used); total usable reserves £75.3m at March 2027 (forecast, pre-overspend); earmarked reserves £48.4m
findings.quote: No drawdowns have been made against this in the Quarter 1 position at a directorate level, but it is evident that the full updated amount will be needed to be utilised in-year. Given the fact it is unlikely that the Q1 overspend position of £13.6m will be brought back in line with budget by year-end, further drawdowns from other earmarked reserves to support the overall Council outturn figure will be needed; however any use of reserves must be replenished.

findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block deficit of £110m with government support programme ended and council facing 10% contribution liability from 2026/27 onwards
findings.detail: The cumulative DSG deficit will reach approximately £110m by end of Q1. The government's Safety Valve programme ended in February 2026. Government has indicated it will fund 90% of historic deficit (approximately £72m) in 2026/27, but this is subject to agreement of a plan with the DfE (decision expected September 2026). The council will be responsible for 10% of deficits, estimated at £13m cumulative to March 2028. The council currently funds £3.5-4m annually just to manage this deficit, a cost that cannot be charged to DSG.
findings.matters: This represents a significant contingent liability for the council. The loss of government support programme and assumption of 10% deficit liability creates an ongoing cost that will constrain the council's flexibility for years. The decision from DfE in September 2026 could materially worsen the position.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit c£110m; government assumed to fund 90% (£72m); council responsible for 10% (£13m cumulative to March 2028); in-year overspend at Q1 £28.7m; annual management cost £3.5-4m
findings.quote: Overall DSG balances at the start of the financial year was a deficit of £80.3m. This is due to the High Needs block deficit (HNB). The projected outturn position for the HNB in year at Q1 is a further in year overspend of £28.7m which will initially increase the cumulative DSG deficit to c£110.0m, but expected to be reduced to around £35m following an assumed payment from the DfE of 90% of the historic deficit.

findings.headline: £8m of approved savings programme not delivered, representing 42% of the reported overspend
findings.detail: Within the £18.9m underlying overspend, £8m is attributed to slippage and non-delivery of the approved savings programme. In Adults alone, £4.1m of £8.6m brought-forward savings remain undelivered. The paper identifies this as a significant ongoing financial risk to the Directorate. If these savings were delivered as planned, the overspend would be reduced substantially.
findings.matters: Failed delivery of savings plans indicates implementation or execution problems beyond just budget pressures. It suggests the council may not achieve future savings targets either, weakening confidence in financial recovery plans.
findings.figures: £8m of £18.9m underlying overspend due to savings non-delivery; Adults Directorate has £4.1m of £8.6m brought-forward savings undelivered
findings.quote: Within this position, an estimated £8m is due to slippage and non-delivery of the approved savings programme across the Council. The delivery of these savings continues to represent a significant financial risk to the Directorate and if not monitored closely have the potential to add the projected £10.7m Directorate overspend.

findings.headline: Adults and Children combined social care overspend of £19m driven by increased complexity and demand, not just inflation, indicating structural cost growth
findings.detail: Adults & Health forecasting £10.7m overspend and Children's Services £8.3m overspend. The paper identifies that over two years, increased care complexity alone has added approximately £11.5m in costs. Children's placements are 50 vs 35 budgeted (50% above budget) at £7.2k per week. The council had added £15.2m for adults and £5.5m for children specifically to address rising care costs, but this proved insufficient.
findings.matters: If cost growth is driven by increasing complexity and demand rather than one-off inflation, the trend will not reverse. This suggests ongoing structural budget pressures in future years and raises questions about the sustainability of service provision.
findings.figures: Adults overspend £10.7m on £171m budget (6.3%); Children overspend £8.3m on £95.2m budget (8.7%); care complexity increased costs by approximately £11.5m over two years; children's external residential placements 50 vs 35 budgeted at £7.2k per week
findings.quote: Initial analysis of expenditure trends suggests that increasing complexity of need is the most significant contributor to the overspend. Over a two-year period, changes in service user complexity are estimated to have increased costs by approximately £11.5m. Care package price increases are estimated to have added a further £0.7m.

findings.headline: Q1 forecast overspend of £13.6m represents significant deterioration from prior year and is explicitly described as unsustainable
findings.detail: The 2026/27 Q1 overspend projection of £13.6m (after using £5.2m strategic contingency reserve) represents a major worsening compared to 2025/26's Q1 projection of £5.9m. The paper explicitly states this position is not sustainable. The council will need to use additional reserves to balance the budget, which must then be replenished in 2027/28, constraining future financial flexibility.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand if the council can sustain its financial position without depleting reserves. The scale and trajectory of the overspend, combined with the need to replenish reserves, indicates structural budget problems.
findings.figures: Q1 2026/27 forecast overspend £13.6m (compared to Q1 2025/26 forecast of £5.9m); strategic contingency reserve of £5.2m; total usable reserves £75.3m
findings.quote: This current forecast overspend is not affordable to the Council both in year and the implications such an overspend has for future budgets. Should there be an overspend, which is considered highly probable, at the end of 2026/27 then the Council will need to utilise reserves to balance. These reserves will need to be replenished in 2027/28.

findings.headline: The council's statutory accounting protection for pooled investment fund losses expires in 2029, exposing a £1.3 million accumulated loss to the General Fund.
findings.detail: The council holds £10m in the CCLA Local Authorities Property Fund. This investment has unrealised cumulative losses of £1.3m, currently protected by a government statutory override on accounting for pooled fund gains and losses. MHCLG has indicated this override will only extend until 1 April 2029 for investments held before April 2024. After that date, any losses will be recognised in the Surplus or Deficit statement and impact General Fund balances directly.
findings.matters: A material unrealised loss will eventually become a revenue charge against balances, reducing the council's financial flexibility. The council should plan for this £1.3m impact or consider whether the property fund investment remains appropriate.
findings.figures: Investment £10.0m; unrealised cumulative losses £1.3m; statutory override expires 1 April 2029
findings.quote: Unrealised cumulative capital losses of £1.3 million will not have an impact on the General Fund as the Council is utilising a government statutory override for pooled investment funds... Following the end of the statutory override, any gains or losses arising on these investments will be recognised in the Surplus or Deficit on the Provision of Services and will therefore impact General Fund balances.

findings.headline: A temporary breach of the council's £10 million counterparty lending limit with Barclays raised governance concerns, though it was resolved within one day.
findings.detail: An overnight balance of £10.6m with Barclays temporarily exceeded the council's £10m limit for a single counterparty. The breach was caused by unexpected late receipts combined with payment authorisation limits. It was resolved the following day with senior officer approval and caused no financial loss, but it indicates potential gaps in operational controls.
findings.matters: Counterparty limits exist to manage credit concentration risk. Any breach, even temporary and resolved, suggests controls may not be fully automated or may lack sufficient safeguards against late-day processing errors.
findings.figures: Balance £10.6m exceeded limit of £10.0m
findings.quote: On one occasion during the year, unexpected late receipts combined with payment authorisation limits resulted in a one-day overnight balance of £10.6 million with Barclays, temporarily exceeding the £10.0 million counterparty limit. The position was resolved the following day and all actions were taken with senior officer approval.

findings.headline: Long-term borrowing costs have risen sharply despite Bank Rate cuts, forcing the council to shift towards short-term borrowing at higher immediate rates.
findings.detail: PWLB rates increased significantly: 10-year rates rose from 5.42% to 5.72%, and 20-year rates from 5.91% to 6.23%. The council's average borrowing rate increased from 4.26% to 4.42%. The council is now deliberately using short-to-medium term borrowing to avoid locking in high long-term rates, but rates for short-term borrowing reached 5.0-7.0% at year-end. This strategy accepts refinancing risk to manage costs.
findings.matters: Rising long-term rates increase the cost of council borrowing. The shift to short-term borrowing reduces upfront costs but creates refinancing risk if rates remain elevated when loans mature.
findings.figures: 10-year PWLB rate 5.42% → 5.72%; 20-year PWLB rate 5.91% → 6.23%; average council borrowing rate 4.26% → 4.42%
findings.quote: The increase in long term rates, despite a drop in the base rate, reflects the premium borrowers are facing to lock in costs against such an uncertain backdrop and therefore means the Council is currently focusing on short to medium term borrowing to fund the capital plan.

findings.headline: Total external borrowing increased by £42.8 million in a single year to £816.8 million, with further large increases projected.
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) grew from £848.8m to £903.5m in 2025-26 and is projected to reach £1,099.1m by 2027 and £1,191.0m by 2028. The liability benchmark shows the council will need significantly more borrowing in coming years to fund its capital programme. The council took £90m from PWLB and £67.5m from other local authorities, both described as 'in line with expectations'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's total indebtedness trajectory and whether the growing capital programme and associated borrowing remain sustainable and affordable.
findings.figures: External borrowing £816.8m (up from £774.0m); CFR £903.5m (up from £848.8m); projected CFR £1,099.1m (2027) and £1,191.0m (2028)
findings.quote: Total external borrowing at 31 March 2026 increased by £42.8 million to £816.8 million (£774.0 million as at 31 March 2025). This was in line with expectations and planned borrowing as per forecasted update.

findings.headline: Internal audit continues to report concerns over contract management, data management and cash handling controls
findings.detail: While overall assurance levels improved over 2024/25, the Head of Audit noted that some concerns persist in three key areas: contract management, data and information management, and cash handling. The council is implementing a new contract management framework and training, with CGAC to receive a report on exemptions and breaches in 2026.
findings.matters: Persistent control weaknesses in contract management and financial controls (cash handling) over multiple audit cycles suggest supervisory gaps. These are areas where councils have historically seen fraud or significant overspends.
findings.figures: Concerns flagged in contract management, data management, cash handling
findings.quote: Some concerns persist in contract management, data and information management, and cash handling.

findings.detail: The external auditor's 2024/25 report (approved January 2026) retained three key recommendations from the prior year. While acknowledging positive improvements in the council's overall financial position, the auditor continued to identify financial sustainability, SEND, and housing regulatory issues as valid concerns at the end of 2025/26.
findings.matters: Persistence of the same audit recommendations across years indicates systemic issues that management action has not yet resolved. Continued flagging of financial sustainability as a concern is material to credit assessment.

findings.quote: The external auditor continued to identify the issues of financial sustainability, SEND and Housing Regulatory as valid at the end of 2025/26.

findings.headline: New significant governance issue: absence of Leader and Cabinet following May 2026 elections creates directional uncertainty
findings.detail: The council's leadership structure was disrupted by the May 2026 elections, with no formal Leader or Cabinet in place. The Chief Executive is acting as Leader. This is explicitly identified as a new significant governance issue that may create problems around organizational direction.
findings.matters: Leadership continuity is critical for strategic decision-making and financial planning. An interregnum creates uncertainty about priorities and decisions, particularly during a period of financial constraint.

The council is conducting an ongoing review of the capital programme to ensure it remains affordable, and a further refresh is planned as part of the MTFP update in late summer 2026.
findings.matters: A £91m slippage (30%) suggests either reduced affordability or delivery capacity issues. Ongoing reviews for affordability indicate the council may need to constrain future capital plans.

findings.headline: Revenue budget: 63% of £30m planned savings delivered; persistent social care overspends remain
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget included £30m of savings but only 63% were achieved. The council managed a projected Q3 overspend of £4.1m down to £1.8m outturn, but did so by drawing on reserves in the short term. Social care continues to be a significant pressure area. The 2026/27 budget allocated additional funding for demand pressures to reduce the scale of in-year variations.
findings.matters: Savings plans consistently underdelivering (37% miss rate) and reliance on reserves to balance the budget indicates structural spending pressures rather than one-off issues. Social care is a growing demand-led pressure.

findings.headline: Housing regulator inspection underway following formal notice in 2024; 1,624 fire safety actions overdue as of March 2026
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing issued a formal notice in March 2024 over damp, mould, condensation and fire safety. The council reduced damp cases from 1,200 to 400, but fire risk assessments identified 9,750 actions, of which 3,015 remain outstanding and 1,624 are overdue as of March 2026. A planned inspection will commence end June 2026 with grading expected September 2026. Phase 2 of Awaab's Law requiring action on serious hazards begins October 2026.
findings.matters: Ongoing regulatory intervention on a material asset (housing stock), with an active inspection in progress and a hard October 2026 deadline for Phase 2 compliance. Overdue fire safety actions create operational and liability risk.
findings.figures: 1,200 damp/mould cases reduced to 400; 9,750 fire risk actions identified; 3,015 outstanding (1,624 overdue) as of March 2026
findings.quote: The Regulator of Social Housing issued formal notice in March 2024, identifying areas where the Council needs to improve its compliance, specifically for the treatment of damp, mould and condensation and fire safety.

findings.headline: SEND deficit grew to £81.3m and costs £4m annually to service, with March 2028 deadline to eradicate it
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit increased from £63.8m at March 2025 to £81.3m at March 2026. The DfE will fund 90% through a grant, but the council is responsible for the remaining 10%. The statutory override allowing the deficit ends March 2028, by which point it must be eliminated. The council is developing refreshed DSG recovery trajectories and a plan to the DfE due by June 2026.
findings.matters: A growing £81m deficit that costs £4m annually to service is a significant drain on resources, and the hard March 2028 deadline means the council must find funds to eliminate the remaining 10% of the deficit within 18 months.
findings.figures: £81.3m deficit at 31 March 2026 (£63.8m at 31/3/25); £4m pa in servicing costs; council responsible for 10% of deficit after DfE grant

findings.detail: Adults and Health directorate projecting £4m variance against £14.3m target (28% shortfall). Care homes market review alone £1.5m over budget; domiciliary care and respite frameworks also slipping. Multiple items rated 'slipped' with lower confidence in mitigating actions, with work rolling into 2026-27.
