findings.paper_title: App 2 - 25-26 - Monthly Budget Savings Delivery Update - Q3
findings.headline: Council will miss £6.8m of £30.6m budgeted savings, rising to £9.2m including unrecovered prior-year slippage.
findings.detail: At quarter 3, projected full-year delivery is £23.8m against £30.6m budgeted (23% shortfall). Prior-year savings not achieved add £2.4m to the gap, bringing total variance to £9.2m. The council is offsetting parts of this shortfall with reserve drawdowns to balance the year.
findings.matters: Consistent inability to deliver planned savings signals either unrealistic financial planning or operational delivery challenges that impact the council's ability to meet medium-term financial plans and debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: Budgeted savings £30.6m, projected delivery £23.8m (variance £6.8m), prior-year slippage £2.4m, total variance £9.2m

findings.headline: Capital plan re-profiled by £14.7m with slippage pushed into future years, signalling delivery challenges
findings.detail: The 2025/26 capital budget has reduced by £14.7m since the Council Budget Report, comprising £14.2m of identified slippage re-profiled into future years (£11.6m General Fund, £2.6m HRA) and a £0.5m loss of UKSPF grant.
findings.matters: Capital slippage indicates execution challenges in delivering planned schemes; re-profiling moves pressure into future years and suggests the capital programme may be front-loaded with optimistic delivery assumptions.
findings.figures: £14.7m net reduction in 2025/26 capital budget, £14.2m slippage (£11.6m GF, £2.6m HRA), £0.5m UKSPF grant loss
findings.quote: Since the Council Budget Report the 2025/26 capital budget has reduced by a further £14.7m. This consists of identified slippage of £14.2m (General Fund £ 11.6m, HRA £ 2.6m) being re -profiled into subsequent financial years and a decrease in UKSPF grant allocation of £0.5m within the Highways Capital Plan.

findings.headline: Asset sale delays at Castle Grange and Claremont House care homes creating expected savings slippage
findings.detail: The sale of Castle Grange and Claremont House care homes has been delayed, creating an adverse variance in expected savings that is being covered by one-off contingency funding rather than asset proceeds.
findings.matters: A delayed asset sale indicates the council cannot execute planned divestments on schedule, forcing it to plug gaps through reserves rather than capital proceeds, and potentially reducing future capital availability.
findings.figures: Amount not separately quantified, covered by contingency reserve draw
findings.quote: There is also an adverse variance in relation to Castle Grange and Claremont House care homes which is being covered by one -off funding from the budget contingency reserve – the delay in their sale has resulted in a slippage in the expected saving against the assumed levels within Adult Social Care and Place.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit of £81.3m locking up cash and creating borrowing constraints
findings.detail: The DSG deficit has reached £81.3m cumulatively, with a £17.5m in-year overspend at Q3. The council must fund this deficit from cash balances that could otherwise be deployed to manage capital borrowing. The council estimates holding this deficit costs £3.8m per annum at 5% interest. The Statutory Override allowing the deficit to be carried forward ends March 2028, though government has committed to funding 90% of historic deficits accrued to March 2026.
findings.matters: An £81.3m deficit is immobilizing a substantial portion of the council's cash reserves, directly constraining its borrowing headroom for capital programmes and creating a hard deadline (March 2028) for resolution.
findings.figures: £81.3m cumulative DSG deficit, £17.5m in-year overspend at Q3, £2.15m per annum Safety Valve contribution for 5 years from 2025/26, £3.8m estimated cost of holding deficit at 5%
findings.quote: The projected outturn position for the DSG at Q 3 is an in year overspend of £17.5m which will increase the cumulative deficit to £81.3m. The deficit has a significant impact upon Council cash flows as it has to fund this deficit from existing balances, which it could have ordinarily used to help manage borrowing on the capital plan.

findings.headline: Home to School Transport £2.1m pressure requiring contingency now and permanent budget increase next year
findings.detail: The council is forecasting £2.1m of pressure in Home to School Transport costs, currently being managed through Strategic Budget contingency reserve in 2025/26 but requiring additional permanent budget allocation in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A cost line growing enough to need contingency funding in year and a permanent budget increase in the following year indicates either volume growth or unit cost inflation the council cannot absorb.
findings.figures: £2.1m Home to School Transport pressure
findings.quote: Pressures of c£2.1m in relation to the cost of Home to School Transport are forecast. It is proposed that the Strategic Budget contingency reserve is used to mitigate this pressure in 2025/26 and additional budget provision will be made in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £3.7m with residential care homes showing £7.8m pressure
findings.detail: Adults & Health is projecting £3.7m overspend after central reserves. Residential and Nursing care home placements show an overspend of £7.8m, with Independent Homecare adding £1.1m pressure, only partially offset by underspends in other areas.
findings.matters: Large overruns in adult care placement costs indicate either rising unit costs from providers or volume growth; both signal demand pressures likely to persist and grow as the adult population ages.
findings.figures: £3.7m Adults & Health overspend, £7.8m residential/nursing placements overspend, £1.1m Independent Homecare overspend
findings.quote: The overall projected position for the Adults & Health Directorate is an overspend of £3.7m, after use of budget contingency/inflation reserves.

findings.headline: Children's Services £7m overspend driven by External Residential Placements at rising cost per placement
findings.detail: Children's Services is forecasting £7m pressure (after central reserves), up £2.5m from Q2. The core driver is External Residential Placements: 42 children in care at an average cost of £6.7K per week. The paper explicitly notes 'there is potential for the figures to rise', with 645 Looked After Children in the system.
findings.matters: This represents demand-led cost pressures the council cannot control; rising average placement costs and acknowledged potential for further growth indicate a service trajectory that will worsen unless placement volumes drop.
findings.figures: 42 External Residential Placements at £6.7K per week average, 645 Looked After Children
findings.quote: The projected outturn position for Children's Services at Q3 is pressure of £7m (after use of central reserves), an increase of £2.5m since Q2. The main reasons for the current projected position are demand led pressures primarily in the cost and number of External Residential Placements (ERPs). As at Q3, there were 42 External Residential Placements, and the average placement cost has increased to £6.7K p/w. These are being managed carefully, but there is potential for the figures to rise.

findings.headline: £8.7m of overspend driven by slippage in approved savings programme, signalling execution risk
findings.detail: The £4.1m overspend is heavily weighted towards £8.7m of delays in delivering the approved savings programme across the council, partially offset by £4.6m of business-as-usual underspends. This indicates the budget relied on cost control measures that are not materializing on schedule.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council can execute planned savings; large slippage suggests budget assumptions may be optimistic and underlying control is weaker than forecast.
findings.figures: £8.7m savings slippage, £4.6m business-as-usual underspends offsetting
findings.quote: Within this position, an estimated £8.7m is due to slippage in the approved savings programme across the Council. There is a projected £4.6m of net underspends on business as usual activities.

findings.headline: General Fund overspend of £4.1m with budget contingency reserve completely depleted to nil balance
findings.detail: Kirklees is forecasting a £4.1m General Fund overspend after deploying £5.5m from the budget contingency reserve. The contingency, which opened at £3.5m, has been drawn to nil by Q3. Without further action, any remaining overspend at year end will be funded from general reserves.
findings.matters: Complete depletion of contingency reserves signals the council has exhausted its short-term financial cushion and has reduced flexibility to absorb unexpected pressures or demand variations.
findings.figures: £4.1m forecast overspend, £5.5m contingency used, nil contingency balance remaining
findings.quote: the projected outturn position at Q3 is a forecast overspend of £4.1m after the use of £5.5m of the budget contingency reserve. The remaining £0.2m was drawn down from the Strategic Budget Contingency reserve at Quarter 3 leaving a nil balance.

findings.headline: £7.3m in new savings required for 2026/27, lowest in three years but ongoing structural need
findings.detail: The council still needs to identify £7.3m in efficiency savings to balance 2026/27, though this is lower than prior years. Savings focus on management and administration rather than frontline services, but ongoing requirement indicates unresolved structural pressures.
findings.matters: Persistent need for savings (even if declining) signals underlying budget pressures; if savings delivery slips or demand accelerates, budget gaps would re-emerge
findings.figures: £7.3m new savings required, lowest in 3 years
findings.quote: The plans include £7.3m in new revenue savings. This is the lowest savings requirement for the last three years and demonstrates the increasing sustainability of the budget. Savings are primarily focused on reducing the management and administration costs of services and retaining posts that are already vacant.

findings.headline: Business rates income forecast includes £6m provision for appeals from 2026 revaluation, creating collection risk
findings.detail: Following the 2026 business rates revaluation, the council expects high levels of ratepayer appeals. The budget includes £6m provision for repayments for successful appeals, but the actual level of appeals is inherently uncertain.
findings.matters: Business rates volatility creates budget uncertainty; if appeals exceed the £6m provision, the council faces unbudgeted income pressure
findings.figures: £6m appeals provision, 97.5% collection rate assumed, gross rates payable £159m
findings.quote: For 2026/27, appeals are likely to be high due to increased Rateable Values for many hereditaments resulting from the 2026 revaluation, however it is extremely difficult to estimate how many businesses will ultimately lodge a successful appeal. Due to this uncertainty, the updated budget figures include the Government estimate of the likely level of appeals nationally. For Kirklees, this high-level estimate equates to repayments to ratepayers of approximately £6m with respect to the 2026/27 liability.

findings.headline: Council committed to £10.6m SEND Safety Valve contribution over 5 years from 2025/26
findings.detail: The council has agreed to contribute £10.6m total to the SEND Safety Valve plan, starting with £2.15m in 2025/26 and continuing at the same level for four years. This is a new multi-year commitment for education-related service pressures.
findings.matters: Multi-year commitments to demand-led spending reduce financial flexibility and are difficult to unwind; if demand increases or exceeds forecasts, this creates pressure
findings.figures: £10.6m total, £2.15m annually from 2025/26 for 5 years
findings.quote: The strategy also recognises the need to provide the Council's agreed contribution to the SEND Safety Valve plan at c£10.6m, the first contribution is being made as budgeted in 2025/26 at £2.15m and the following four years assume the same level.

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget balance depends on £14m one-time government funding from Fair Funding Review 2.0
findings.detail: The balanced 2026/27 budget relies on £14m of additional unringfenced government funding from Fair Funding Review 2.0, which implements 100% Council Tax equalisation. This funding increase is not guaranteed to continue at the same level in future years.
findings.matters: Budget plans dependent on government policy changes create downside risk; if funding reforms are reversed or reduced, the council would face immediate new savings requirements
findings.figures: £14m additional un-ringfenced funding, 8.1% CSP increase for Kirklees (vs 6.1% national average)
findings.quote: Changes to central government funding are benefiting Kirklees with an increase in un-ringfenced funding of c£14m in 2026/27. In part, this is due to the implementation of 100% Council Tax equalisation through the Fair Funding review 2.0.

findings.headline: 2025/26 overspend of £5.1m at Q2, forecast to reduce to less than £3.5m, indicates current-year management challenges
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £5.1m overspend for 2025/26 at quarter 2, with Q3 showing some improvement to less than £3.5m. Current-year overspends typically require reserve drawdowns or in-year management action.
findings.matters: Current-year overspends reduce financial flexibility and often require reserve depletion, eroding the council's cushion for future shocks
findings.figures: £5.1m overspend Q2, forecast improvement to less than £3.5m Q3
findings.quote: Updated figures in this report also reflect that the Council is forecasting a £5.1m overspend for 2025/26 at Quarter 2 (the draft Quarter 3 position shows an improvement to a projected overspend of less than £3.5m)

findings.headline: Adult and children's social care demand pressures continue, requiring £20.7m additional funding
findings.detail: The council has allocated £15.2m additional for adult social care and £5.5m for children's services in 2026/27. These pressures are described as an ongoing national issue expected to continue beyond 2026/27, consuming most of the available budget headroom.
findings.matters: Demand-led services growing faster than overall budget growth indicate structural budget pressure and declining flexibility to absorb further cost increases
findings.figures: £15.2m adult social care, £5.5m children's services
findings.quote: A major part of the pressure on council budgets has been due to increased demand for services, especially for social care for both adults and children. This is an ongoing national issue. The draft budget addresses these demands with an additional £15.2m for adult social care and an extra £5.5m for children who need extra support.

findings.headline: £30m LOBO loans (3.8% of debt) face refinancing risk if lenders exercise call options; council will repay rather than accept higher rates
findings.detail: The council holds £30m of LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans where lenders can call the loans at set dates and propose new interest rates, with the council able to repay at no cost or accept the new rate. With interest rates currently elevated, lenders are highly likely to exercise these call options. The council's policy is to repay LOBO loans if rates are increased, forcing refinancing that may not be timed or priced optimally and reducing flexibility in debt management.
findings.matters: Forced refinancing of £30m at times and rates not of the council's choosing increases refinancing risk and could push debt costs above budget. This reduces flexibility to manage debt costs and increases vulnerability to adverse market conditions at refinancing dates.
findings.figures: £30m LOBO loans; 3.8% of total debt
findings.quote: With interest rates remaining high, there is a good chance that lenders will exercise their options. If they do, the Council will take the option to repay loans to reduce refinancing risk in later years.

findings.headline: Service loans to regeneration schemes carry significant loss provisions; £12.2m HD1 Living loan for 103 New Street has £8.7m provision (71% of exposure), indicating substantial credit risk
findings.detail: The council holds £42.1m of service loans with total loss provisions of £9.1m (21% of portfolio). The largest exposure is within a £24.4m 'local businesses and charities' category, which includes a £12.2m loan to HD1 Living for the 103 New Street student accommodation regeneration project carrying £8.7m loss provision (71%), and £7.5m relating to Kingsgate shopping centre (repaid in full December 2025). High loss provisions suggest schemes may not be performing as expected or face substantial credit risk. Kirklees College also holds a £12.6m loan with £0.3m provision.
findings.matters: High loss provisions on major regeneration loans indicate credit risk or operational difficulties with schemes. This affects both the council's ability to recover the loans and its expected economic returns from capital investment in these schemes. A lender would want to understand why 103 New Street carries a 71% loss provision and assess the viability of ongoing regeneration lending.
findings.figures: Service loans £42.1m; total loss allowance £9.1m (21%); 103 New Street £12.2m with £8.7m provision (71%); Kingsgate £7.5m repaid December 2025; Kirklees College £12.6m with £0.3m provision
findings.quote: Local businesses and charities 24.4 -8.7 15.8; This is made up of numerous investments, the largest of which is £12.2 million towards 103 New Street and £7.5 million relates to Kingsgate.

findings.headline: Council will borrow £525.6m over three years to fund £326m increase in Capital Financing Requirement driven by major capital projects including Our Cultural Heart, town centre regeneration, and DfE Safety Valve special schools investment
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to grow from £939.3m (31 March 2025) to £1,265.2m by 2029, a 35% increase. This growth is driven by planned capital investments in major regeneration schemes ('Our Cultural Heart'), town and district centre regeneration, two special schools required under the council's DfE Safety Valve intervention agreement, and housing stock investment. To fund this growth, the council will require approximately £525.6 million in additional borrowing over the three-year period to 31 March 2029.
findings.matters: This represents a material expansion of the council's capital programme and debt commitments. A lender would want to verify that major projects (particularly 'Our Cultural Heart') are viable, on track, and capable of generating expected economic benefits and returns to service the additional debt.
findings.figures: £525.6 million new borrowing required over 3 years; CFR growth from £939.3m to £1,265.2m (35% increase); external borrowing £836.0m forecast at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: There is a planned increase in the CFR due to increases in the capital programme, in particular Our Cultural Heart, town and district centre regeneration programmes the investment in two special schools as part of the Council Safety Valve agreement with the DfE and investment in our Housing stock. The Council will be required to borrow up to £525.6 million to fund the increase in the Loans CFR over the 3 year period from 31 March 2026 to 31 March 2029.

findings.headline: Council forecasted funding gains of £6.7m in 2026-27 and £5m annually in 2027-28 and 2028-29 from Fair Funding Review, but Government's detailed proposals remain unresolved.
findings.detail: The council took a prudent approach in forecasting medium-term funding gains from equalisation and Fair Funding Review: £6.7m in 2026-27 and £5m annually in 2027-28 and 2028-29. As at January 2026, the provisional LGFS has confirmed an additional £6m of funding available in 2026-27 beyond the draft budget. However, this is contingent on government reform of the funding system completing as planned, which has not been formally confirmed.
findings.matters: Reliance on uncertain future government funding increases introduces execution risk; delays or changes to funding reform plans would widen the budget gap further.
findings.figures: Forecast gain £6.7m in 2026-27; £5m annually 2027-28 and 2028-29; provisional LGFS additional £6m in 2026-27
findings.quote: The Council is expecting to gain additional funding in the medium-term from equalisation and the Fair Funding Review. The Council took a prudent approach and forecasted funding gains over the next three years of £6.7m in 2026-27, and £5m annually in 2027-28 and 2028-29 within the Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP).

findings.headline: Housing compliance continues as significant weakness: Regulatory Notice from Regulator of Social Housing remains in place at year-end, with fire safety, damp and mould, and water quality issues still outstanding as of June 2025.
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing issued a Regulatory Notice in March 2024 following the council's self-referral. Although the council has made progress (damp and mould reaching business-as-usual, water quality testing 99.8% compliant), the Notice had not been removed by end of year-end 2024-25. Actions around fire, damp, mould and water quality testing remained outstanding as at June 2025. The council is working towards removal by end of 2025 or beginning of 2026.
findings.matters: Regulatory intervention in housing stock indicates governance and operational failings in a major service area. Continued non-compliance creates reputational risk and potential for further regulatory action.
findings.figures: Regulatory Notice issued March 2024; still in place 31 March 2025; water quality testing 99.8% compliant as of June 2025
findings.quote: The Regulator of Social Housing issued a Regulatory Notice in March 2024 following the Council's self-referral. The Council has been on an improvement journey and, whilst there has been significant progress, the Council is aware it needs to continue strengthening arrangements.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan shows budget gap of £30.2m over six-year period to 2030-31, with largest shortfall of £17.9m in 2026-27.
findings.detail: The council's updated MTFP (December 2025) indicates an estimated budget gap of £30.2m over the period 2025-26 to 2030-31. The council is expecting additional funding from equalisation and the Fair Funding Review (£6.7m in 2026-27, £5m annually in 2027-28 and 2028-29 based on prudent forecasts, with provisional LGFS providing additional £6m in 2026-27), but the scale of the gap remains substantial.
findings.matters: A multi-year structural budget gap of this size indicates the council will need to deliver significant service reductions, asset sales, or find additional external funding beyond currently projected grants.
findings.figures: Estimated budget gap £30.2m to 2030-31; largest shortfall £17.9m in 2026-27
findings.quote: The Council's latest Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP) from December 2025, which covers a six-year period from 2025-26 to 2030-31, indicated an estimated budget gap of £30.2m over the period to 2030-31.

findings.headline: Council reserves sit at £25m general and £36m earmarked (£61m total), which the auditor describes as low and below the council's own desirable level of £31m.
findings.detail: The council's general reserve of £25m sits above the calculated minimum of £22m but below the desirable level of £31m. Earmarked reserves stand at £36m. The auditor notes that reserves are low in comparison to revenue expenditure and when compared to other metropolitan authorities. The council has committed to adding £1m annually to general reserves from 2025-26 to 2030-31, but has not yet demonstrated ability to increase reserves sustainably given ongoing revenue overspends.
findings.matters: Low reserves constrain the council's ability to absorb financial shocks, service disruptions, or demand surges without increasing borrowing or cutting services.
findings.figures: General reserve £25m (minimum £22m, desirable £31m); earmarked reserves £36m; total £61m
findings.quote: We have identified concerns around the Council's reserve levels, which are low compared to revenue expenditure and when compared to other metropolitan authorities.

findings.headline: Transformation savings programme in Adults and Health underdelivered by £3.4m (41% of target) in 2024-25, at a time when the council needs £30.2m cumulative savings over the MTFP.
findings.detail: The Adults and Health directorate was tasked with delivering £8.2m in transformation savings in 2024-25 but only achieved £4.828m (59.1%). Overall, the council delivered £33.7m of £42.6m budgeted savings (79%). The auditor has raised a key recommendation that the council should identify set transformation targets and report them clearly, as transformation efficiency delivery is key to setting the council on a sustainable footing.
findings.matters: If the council's transformation programme cannot deliver planned savings when demand and cost pressures are acute, there is no clear path to closing the estimated £30.2m budget gap over the MTFP period.
findings.figures: Adults transformation: delivered £4.828m of £8.2m target (59.1%); overall savings delivery £33.7m of £42.6m (79%); cumulative budget gap £30.2m to 2030-31
findings.quote: In 2024-25, the Council delivered £33.7m (79%) in savings against a budgeted target of £42.6m. Slippage was driven by a lack of delivery within the adults and health transformation programme - of the initial target of £8.2m identified, £4.828m (59.1%) was delivered at year-end.

findings.headline: Council delivered £5.6m revenue overspend in 2024-25 despite use of £1.5m demand reserve, with services overspending by £13.5m.
findings.detail: The council overspent by £5.6m net, funded from earmarked reserves. Underlying service overspends were £13.5m (Place £6.3m, Children and Families £5.7m, Adults and Health £1.3m), partially offset by an £8m underspend in corporate budgets. Q2 2025-26 is forecasting a £5.1m overspend. The auditor considers the council has not yet demonstrated financial sustainability.
findings.matters: Persistent year-on-year overspends depleting reserves, even when the council is implementing cost controls, suggests underlying service demand or cost pressures are not being matched by funding or savings.
findings.figures: £5.6m net revenue overspend 2024-25; services overspent £13.5m; Q2 2025-26 forecast £5.1m overspend
findings.quote: In 2024-25, the Council delivered a £5.6m revenue overspend, funded from earmarked reserves. Services overspent by £13.5m in-year, with the largest variances in the Children and Families (£5.7m), and Place (£6.3m) directorates.

findings.headline: DSG deficit of £63.8m now exceeds the council's total usable reserves and is forecast to peak at £72.3m in 2025-26.
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit rose to £63.8m at year-end 2024-25 following an in-year overspend of £20.1m. This deficit is already 105% of the council's total usable reserves (£61.1m). Despite mitigating actions through the Safety Valve Agreement, the deficit is forecast to peak at £72.3m in 2025-26 and remain at £56.3m by the end of the agreement in 2029-30. The council is off-track with agreed Safety Valve targets.
findings.matters: A DSG deficit this large creates a structural cash drain that exceeds available reserves and constrains the council's ability to manage other financial pressures or invest in capital.
findings.figures: Cumulative deficit £63.8m (105% of usable reserves of £61.1m); in-year overspend £20.1m; forecast peak £72.3m in 2025-26; forecast end-position 2029-30 £56.3m
findings.quote: The cumulative deficit stood at £63.8m at the end of 2024-25. This deficit is already 105% of the Council's total usable reserves and is forecast to continue increasing.

findings.headline: £9.3m of investment properties not revalued annually; non-compliance with accounting code requirements
findings.detail: The CIPFA Code requires all investment properties to be revalued annually. £9.3m of investment properties held by the Council have not been subject to annual revaluation. Management treats properties below £250k as de minimis, but the value of the sub-£250k population has risen in recent years and is now approaching the audit's performance materiality threshold of £12.8m, meaning it can no longer be treated as trivial.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with the accounting code means reported investment property values may not reflect fair value. As the de minimis population approaches materiality, this is becoming a more serious exposure.
findings.figures: £9.3m of investment properties; de minimis threshold £250k; audit performance materiality £12.8m
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2025, there were investment properties totalling £9.3m which have not been subject to annual revaluation, which is not compliant with Code requirements. Management asserts that investment properties below £250k are de minimis and trivial to the overall balance of investment property held by the Authority. The value of this sub-£250k population has risen in recent years towards our audit performance materiality threshold of £12.8m.

findings.headline: Cash flow statement includes non-cash transactions in investing and financing sections; recurring audit finding not implemented
findings.detail: Unlike most councils using CIPFA models, Kirklees uses an internally-developed cash flow statement model. The auditor has flagged for two consecutive audit cycles that the statement incorrectly includes non-cash transactions in the investing and financing activity sections. Although the Council agreed the misstatements this year, the auditor has re-raised a recommendation to improve the accuracy of the statement and supporting working papers for 2025-26.
findings.matters: A primary financial statement containing classification errors, even if not materially misstated, indicates weak internal controls over financial reporting and a pattern of not implementing audit recommendations.
findings.figures: Issue identified in prior two audit cycles; recommendation re-raised for 2025-26
findings.quote: During the last two cycles of external audit, we have flagged concerns that the sections of the statement presenting net cash flows for investing activities and financing activities include non-cash-based transactions, which should not be included in these sections. As was the case in the prior year, we have identified misstatements arising from the presentation of this primary accounting statement.

findings.headline: Social Housing Regulator has issued Regulatory Notice for failure to meet statutory health and safety requirements in council homes
findings.detail: The Regulator identified breaches of health and safety standards in some council homes in March 2024. Remedial actions required include fire safety works from assessments, repairs to damp and mould, and water quality testing. While progress has been made on fire works and damp/mould backlog, the auditor notes further progress is still required before the Council can demonstrate compliance with regulatory standards.
findings.matters: A formal regulatory notice indicates the Council's social housing arm is not meeting mandatory safety standards. This creates reputational risk, potential enforcement action, and unbudgeted remediation costs, and reflects operational/governance weakness.
findings.figures: Notice issued March 2024; remedial actions ongoing in 2025-26
findings.quote: In March 2024, the Social Housing Regulator published a Regulatory Notice identifying that the Council was failing to meet statutory health and safety requirements in some council homes. Remedial actions required by the Council to address the issue include: fire remedial actions resulting from fire assessments, repairs to address damp and mould and conducting water quality testing.

findings.headline: Building valuations contain material data errors; extrapolated error of £4.1m from incorrect floor area records
findings.detail: Auditor testing found errors in the gross internal area (GIA) data provided to the valuer. These errors, when extrapolated across the population of buildings valued on a Depreciated Replacement Cost basis, total £4.1m. This is an increase from £3.3m extrapolated error in the prior year. Management has not adjusted the accounts on the grounds that this is an extrapolation rather than a factual error, but the auditor notes this is a recurring issue that must be resolved.
findings.matters: Building valuations (£473m) are a major balance sheet asset. Recurring errors in the core data used to value them undermine confidence in reported asset values and suggest quality-of-records issues in the estates team.
findings.figures: £4.1m extrapolated error in 2024-25 (prior year £3.3m); £473m land and buildings balance
findings.quote: Our valuation testing of floor areas to property records & AutoCAD drawings identified errors in source data provided to the valuer. This error has been extrapolated across the population of DRC assets and the extrapolated error totals £4.1m.

findings.headline: General fund revenue overspend of £5.6m with £13.5m in-year service overspends and £56.3m cumulative budget gap forecast
findings.detail: Services overspent by £13.5m in 2024-25, with Children and Families £5.7m over (despite drawing £1.5m from reserves) and Place £6.3m over. Overall revenue outturn was £5.6m in deficit. The Council faces an estimated cumulative budget gap of £56.3m to 2030-31, driven by demand and cost pressures in social care.
findings.matters: A recurring revenue overspend alongside a forecast £56m+ gap over the next five years signals that service costs are outrunning income structurally. This drives reliance on reserves or borrowing, both constraints for a lender.
findings.figures: £5.6m revenue outturn overspend; £13.5m in-year service overspends; £56.3m cumulative budget gap 2025-31
findings.quote: The revenue outturn in 2024-25 was an overspend of £5.6m. Services overspent by £13.5m in-year, with the largest variances in the Children and Families (£5.7m), and Place (£6.3m) directorates... The Council continues to face significant financial pressures in the short and medium-term as a result of demand and cost pressures within social care, with an estimated cumulative budget gap of £56.3m in the period to 2030-31.

findings.headline: DSG deficit now exceeds total usable reserves and is forecast to continue increasing
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit grew by £20.1m in-year to reach £63.8m cumulatively. This now represents 105% of the Council's total usable reserves. The auditor notes the deficit is forecast to continue increasing despite a renegotiated Safety Valve plan with the Department for Education, and the Council is under-delivering against the agreed management plan.
findings.matters: A DSG deficit this large, already exceeding reserves, represents a structural funding crisis in schools. Lenders depend on reserves as a buffer; this Council has none, and the problem is worsening.
findings.figures: £20.1m in-year overspend; £63.8m cumulative deficit; 105% of total usable reserves
findings.quote: The Council's Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit has also continued to increase, with an in-year overspend of £20.1m. The cumulative deficit stood at £63.8m at the end of 2024-25, compared with the Safety Valve agreement plan of £63.3m. This deficit is already 105% of the Council's total usable reserves and is forecast to continue increasing.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Mgt Mid Year Report 2025-26 Cabinet
findings.headline: Liability benchmark forecasts additional borrowing requirement of £66.2 million for current year, indicating sustained capital financing gap
findings.detail: Beyond the Council's existing external borrowing, the liability benchmark calculation identifies an estimated additional borrowing need of £66.2 million for 2025/26 based on updated capital plans. The benchmark, which represents the cumulative external borrowing required to fund capital and revenue plans while maintaining minimum £30 million cash balances, shows the Council will remain a long-term borrower with continuous additional requirements across the forecast period.
findings.matters: Persistent and growing borrowing requirement indicates structural funding gap in capital program that will sustain elevated borrowing costs and debt service obligations.
findings.figures: £66.2m additional borrowing forecast for 2025/26; liability benchmark £838.1m (31 March 2026), £983.3m (31 March 2027), £1,073.5m (31 March 2028)
findings.quote: The mid-year forecasted liability benchmark, based on updated capital plans, highlights that there is an expectation of additional borrowing of £66.2 million for the year.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Mgt Mid Year Report 2025-26 Cabinet
findings.headline: Internal borrowing more than doubled to £158.2 million as balance sheet resources continue depleting
findings.detail: Internal (over) borrowing grew from £74.8 million (March 2025 actual) to £158.2 million (September 2025 revised forecast). This represents the Council using internal balance sheet resources to cover the gap between its Capital Financing Requirement and external borrowing, rather than borrowing externally. Concurrently, balance sheet resources declined from £133.4 million to £122.0 million. The strategy estimate projected internal borrowing could reach £344.3 million by year-end if the trend continues.
findings.matters: Rapid depletion of balance sheet resources reduces financial flexibility and resilience; eventual exhaustion forces the Council into higher levels of external borrowing at market rates.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £158.2m (Sept 2025 revised forecast) vs £74.8m (March 2025 actual); balance sheet resources £122.0m vs £133.4m
findings.quote: Less actual external borrowing * 774.0 771.9 ... Internal (over) borrowing 74.8 158.2

findings.paper_title: Treasury Mgt Mid Year Report 2025-26 Cabinet
findings.headline: £30 million of LOBO loans face potential mandatory refinancing risk if lenders exercise call options within next 12 months
findings.detail: The Council holds £30 million in LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans where lenders can propose interest rate increases at preset dates. The report states that "there is an increased probability of call options on the LOBOs being exercised by lenders" given current high market rates. Of these, £20.9 million have potential repayment dates in 2025/26. The Council states it will not accept higher rates if called and will instead repay through external borrowing or other local authority loans.
findings.matters: LOBO refinancing requirements could create unexpected borrowing demand at potentially unfavorable rates within 12 months, affecting cash flow and refinancing strategy.
findings.figures: £30.0 million total LOBO loans; £20.9m with potential repayment in 2025/26; market rate context shows 10-year PWLB rate at 5.53%
findings.quote: As market rates remain high, there is an increased probability of call options on the LOBOs being exercised by lenders. No LOBO loans were called during the 6 month period to September 2025, however there remains a possibility they could within the next 12 months

findings.paper_title: Treasury Mgt Mid Year Report 2025-26 Cabinet
findings.headline: Net borrowing increased by £10.2 million in first six months, with forecast to reach £808.1 million by year-end
findings.detail: The Council's net borrowing position grew from £715.4 million at 31 March 2025 to £725.6 million at 30 September 2025. The revised forecast for 31 March 2026 is £808.1 million, representing year-on-year growth of £92.7 million. The liability benchmark projects sustained borrowing growth, reaching £953.3 million by March 2027 and £1,043.5 million by March 2028.
findings.matters: Rapid growth in net borrowing position is a material change to the Council's debt profile and creditworthiness, particularly the multi-year trajectory showing sustained increases.
findings.figures: £725.6m (30 Sept 2025), £808.1m forecast (31 March 2026), £953.3m forecast (31 March 2027), £1,043.5m forecast (31 March 2028)
findings.quote: The Council's net borrowing increased by £10.2 million in the 6 month period, from £715.4 million at 31 March 2025 to £725.6 million at 30 September 2025.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Mgt Mid Year Report 2025-26 Cabinet
findings.headline: Council revised down internal borrowing forecast significantly mid-year, suggesting capital programme reprofiling
findings.detail: The January strategy estimated internal borrowing (use of balance sheet resources) would reach £344.3m by year-end, but the September revision cut this to £158.2m—a reduction of £186m. This suggests material changes to capital spend timing or scope were made mid-year. Internal borrowing increase from £74.8m to £158.2m still represents a net increase but far less than originally planned.
findings.matters: Major mid-year changes to the capital plan can signal either delivery challenges or project slippage, both material for lenders assessing the council's project delivery capability and forecast reliability.
findings.figures: Original forecast (Jan 25): £344.3m internal borrowing; Revised forecast (Sep 25): £158.2m; Actual at March 2025: £74.8m
findings.quote: The mid-year forecasted liability benchmark, based on updated capital plans, highlights that there is an expectation of additional borrowing of £66.2 million for the year.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Mgt Mid Year Report 2025-26 Cabinet
findings.headline: Net borrowing increasing by £92.7m in one year as capital programme drives up financing requirement
findings.detail: Net borrowing has risen from £715.4m at March 2025 to a forecast £808.1m by March 2026. The underlying need to borrow (CFR) is growing from £939.3m to £1012.7m, with the capital programme expecting to require an additional £66.2m of borrowing this year. This trajectory reflects sustained capital investment commitments.
findings.matters: Rising debt burden requires refinancing capacity and consistent access to borrowing markets; lenders will need to see capital programme plans justify this trajectory and that reserves are available to manage timing mismatches.
findings.figures: Net borrowing increase: £92.7m in year; Capital Financing Requirement: £1012.7m (revised Sep 25 forecast); Additional borrowing requirement: £66.2m for 2025/26
findings.quote: The mid-year forecasted liability benchmark, based on updated capital plans, highlights that there is an expectation of additional borrowing of £66.2 million for the year.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Mgt Mid Year Report 2025-26 Cabinet
findings.headline: LOBO refinancing risk crystallizing as market rates remain elevated
findings.detail: The council holds £30 million of LOBO loans where lenders have options to force repricing at set dates. The report identifies that high current market rates have increased the probability of these options being exercised within the next 12 months. If exercised, the council will repay by borrowing from other local authorities or PWLB at current rates, creating refinancing risk at potentially higher costs than the original loan terms.
findings.matters: Forced refinancing of £30m at current PWLB rates (5-6% range) instead of the original LOBO rates would materially increase interest costs and reduce financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £30.0 million of LOBO loans; current PWLB 10-year rate 5.47%, 20-year rate 5.76%
findings.quote: As market rates remain high, there is an increased probability of call options on the LOBOs being exercised by lenders. No LOBO loans were called during the 6 month period to September 2025, however there remains a possibility they could within the next 12 months

findings.detail: The funding breakdown shows General Fund borrowing has increased by £6.872m. This represents an additional funding source alongside self-funded expenditure (£12.114m), grants & contributions (£3.651m), and revenue contributions (£23.861m).
findings.matters: Increased borrowing to fund capital works adds to the council's debt burden and future debt service obligations, affecting financial flexibility and credit metrics.

findings.detail: Under the 'Funding Removal' section, the council is eliminating £1.359m in capital funding. The largest removal is £1,000k from Investment & Modernisation (Corporate Strategy & Public Health), followed by £290k from Libraries and £50k from IT Hardware. These are not re-profiled to future years but removed entirely from the capital programme.
findings.matters: Permanent removal of discretionary modernization and infrastructure funding could constrain the council's ability to maintain assets and signals budget pressures affecting capital investment capacity.

findings.headline: Multiple major capital schemes totalling £28.9m are being deferred to future years, with largest deferrals including Huddersfield Town Centre (£7.9m), Recycling Fleet (£3.3m), and Transforming Cities Fund (£3.0m).
findings.detail: The council's capital budget is being re-profiled with £28.877m of schemes deferred to future years. Huddersfield Town Centre Action Plan is deferred by £7.882m, Recycling Fleet by £3.264m, Transforming Cities Fund by £3.020m, and Waste Management Plant & Infrastructure by £2.226m. These deferrals span multiple service areas including transport, fleet management, waste services, and town centre regeneration.
findings.matters: Large-scale deferment of capital spending across multiple major projects could indicate the council is facing budget constraints or delivery challenges that prevent executing its planned capital programme.
findings.figures: Huddersfield Town Centre Action Plan (7,882), Recycling Fleet (3,264), Transforming Cities Fund (3,020), Waste Management Plant & Infrastructure (2,226), Total Re-profiling (28,877)

findings.headline: £35m capital investment in new sports facility in North Kirklees added to plan with feasibility study still underway
findings.detail: The council has added an indicative £35m capital budget for a new sports and leisure facility to serve Dewsbury and North Kirklees. Only £0.1m feasibility work is planned for 2025/26; construction is scheduled 2028/29–2032/33. The council expects £5m external funding but will need to borrow £30m. The budget notes 'as more information becomes available, the capital plan will be updated accordingly' — suggesting this is preliminary and could change.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if this £30m borrowing commitment is firm or could be delayed/cancelled, and whether external funding will materialise.
findings.figures: £35m total budget for facility. £0.1m feasibility 2025/26. £35m construction 2028/29–2032/33. £5m external funding hoped for, meaning £30m council borrowing.
findings.quote: Until the outcome of these studies is understood, it is difficult to define the total amount of capital required, so an indicative sum of £35m has been added to the plan. There is an expectation that £5m of the budget will be met by external funding to help mitigate against borrowing.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection rate cannot achieve 98.5% target; reduced to 98.25%, losing £0.7m income
findings.detail: Historically the council budgeted for 98.5% collection rate but has not achieved it. Actual collection rates achieved: 97.9% (2021/22) and 98.2% (2020/21). The council is now reducing the target to 98.25%, which means £0.7m less income than originally forecast. This implies weakening ability to collect council tax, possibly due to hardship in the community.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if taxpayers in the area are struggling to pay, and whether collection will continue to deteriorate.
findings.figures: Collection rate reduced from 98.5% to 98.25%. Impact: £0.7m reduction in assumed income.
findings.quote: Historically the budget has assumed an ultimate Council tax collection rate of 98.5%. The Council has not been able to achieve this ultimate target despite having good systems in place to recover debt... It is therefore proposed to reduce this ultimate target rate to 98.25%.

findings.headline: 27 FTE staff redundancies announced with savings proposals dependent on deletion of vacant posts (28 of 55 posts at risk)
findings.detail: New savings proposals will reduce FTE by approximately 55 posts. However, 28 of these can be accommodated by deleting currently vacant posts. This leaves 27 FTE genuinely at risk of redundancy, with formal HR1 notice given. The council notes it may need to offer voluntary redundancy on a case-by-case basis. This indicates restructuring pressure and risk of service delivery impact if deployment of staff does not happen smoothly.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether announced staff reductions are achievable or whether service disruption could impact revenue collection or service performance.
findings.figures: 55 total potential FTE reduction. 28 from vacant post deletion. 27 genuine redundancy risk. HR1 declaration made.
findings.quote: The new budget saving proposals outlined within the 2026/27 budget (and within Appendix D) have a total potential reduction of FTE (Full time equivalent posts) in the region of 55. However, we can mitigate some of this impact by deleting vacant posts that are currently being held in service structures, equating to approximately 28. This means that the number of staff potentially at risk, because of the 2026/27 budget saving proposals, is currently 27.

findings.headline: Reserves being drawn down to support base budget expenditure with withdrawal only eliminated by 2028, not earlier
findings.detail: The council is using £3.2m from Voluntary Revenue Provision reserve in 2026/27 to support base budget. The 2025/26 draw was £6.0m from the same reserve. The council's strategy is to 'remove use of reserves supporting base expenditure by 2028' — a three-year trajectory. This suggests the council still has structural pressure and is not yet achieving a fully sustainable base budget.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council is still using one-off reserves to support recurring spending, meaning base budget is not fully sustainable yet.
findings.figures: £6.0m draw in 2025/26, £3.2m draw in 2026/27 from Voluntary Revenue Provision reserve. General reserve forecast £30m by 2030.
findings.quote: The strategy provides the removal of use of reserves supporting base expenditure by 2028. This is a temporary source of funding that will need to be removed from the base over the life of the MTFS.

findings.headline: Leeds City Region Business Rates Pool dissolved due to baseline reset wiping growth, removing benefit and increasing safety-net risk
findings.detail: The council was part of a business rates pool since 2013 that had been generating surpluses. However, Fair Funding 2.0's business rates baseline reset wipes away all accumulated growth since 2013/14 and increases safety-net threshold to 95%. All members agreed to cease pooling in 2026/27 because there is now 'little chance of a financial benefit being generated' but 'much increased level of risk that individual member authorities require safety net funding.' This removes a potential upside and increases downside risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know this removes an income stream the council had been receiving and increases volatility risk on retained business rates.
findings.figures: £200k budget added to support Local Plan to compensate for loss of pool surplus previously set aside.
findings.quote: The aforementioned baseline reset also increases the risk that one or more of the authorities will fall into safety net if their business rates income falls. Within the changes there is also an expectation that Government will raise the safety net threshold to 95% of the new Baseline Funding for all authorities (previously 92.5%) which further increases this risk... As such, there has been agreement from all members of the 2025/26 Pool that the pooling arrangements will not be continued into 2026/27.

findings.headline: Government funding settlement assumptions (Fair Funding Review 2.0) remain unconfirmed and settlements could force emergency savings in February
findings.detail: The budget assumes council will receive 60% of modelled funding gain from Fair Funding 2.0 and assumes various grants will roll into Revenue Support Grant. The Draft LGFS is expected mid-December, final settlement before February budget. If the final settlement is lower than assumed or brings new burdens not accounted for, the council has explicitly stated it will need to bring forward 'further savings proposals at speed' from directorates in February.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know this council's budget has material assumptions that are not yet confirmed, and downside risk could force emergency additional cuts.
findings.figures: Assumes 60% gain from Fair Funding 2.0. £68.4m of grants assumed to roll into RSG. Government funding uplift assumed c5% in 2026/27.
findings.quote: Should the final LGFS settlement be at a level lower than the assumptions contained in this report or additional funding assumed comes with new burdens that has not been recognised, then further savings proposals will need to be brought forward at speed from Directorates to enable a balanced budget to be set.

findings.headline: £6.9m of new savings are integral to the balanced budget but represent highest-risk component if not delivered
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget explicitly depends on delivering £6.9m in new savings. These proposals include £2.5m from Children's Services, £2.0m from Adults & Health, £1.3m from Place, and £1.8m from Public Health/Corporate Resources. The savings are focused on management costs and vacant post deletions, but any failure to deliver these forces the council into deficit.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess delivery risk on savings. The council's ability to set a balanced budget for February 2026 depends on these being approved and achievable.
findings.figures: £6.9m total new savings required for 2026/27. £3.1m existing savings already approved. £10.7m total savings (including previously approved).
findings.quote: Note that the Proposed Budget for 2026/27 presented in this report is based on the approval and delivery of £6.9m of new savings for 2026/27 as identified in this report (Appendix D).

findings.headline: Adult Social Care market rates for external providers are still being negotiated with no agreement on uplifts
findings.detail: The budget acknowledges continued uncertainty about rates paid to external care providers. The council notes 'discussions around the uplifts on the rates paid to external providers for demand-led activities are ongoing and will consider the pressure on the market as well as the available funding envelope.' This means the £15.2m additional funding for ASC demand pressures may be insufficient if market rates move faster than assumed.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if provider rate inflation could exceed budget assumptions, forcing further cuts to other services.
findings.figures: £15.2m additional funding for ASC (including c£5.6m for NLW). £2m of additional new savings proposed for ASC.
findings.quote: The economic landscape continues to bring uncertainty within the Adult Social Care market. Continued review remains key, alongside dialogue with key partners. Discussions around the uplifts on the rates paid to external providers for demand-led activities are ongoing and will consider the pressure on the market as well as the available funding envelope.

findings.headline: National Living Wage pressure of £5.6m is still unconfirmed and could force further cuts if higher than assumed
findings.detail: The Adult Social Care budget assumes a National Living Wage increase to £12.71 per hour (from £12.21), costing £5.6m. This rate is not confirmed and will be announced in the Chancellor's budget on 26 November 2025 — after this Cabinet meeting. If the NLW is higher, the council has no buffer to absorb this pressure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if key budget assumptions are still uncertain, and whether there is contingency if pressure materialises.
findings.figures: £5.6m estimated cost of NLW rise to £12.71/hour. Current rate £12.21/hour.
findings.quote: Current budget modelling is based on a rise in the NLW to £12.71 per hour, from the current £12.21 per hour. This is estimated to cost c£5.6m. The NLW rate is expected to be confirmed in the Chancellor's budget on 26th November.

findings.headline: Current year overspend of £5.1m in 2025/26 will require use of reserves or impact on reserves planned for 2026/27
findings.detail: At Quarter 2 2025/26 (reported in this December budget), the council is already forecasting a £5.1m overspend. The budget assumes drawing down £3.2m from Voluntary Revenue Provision reserve in 2026/27. If the 2025/26 overspend is not recovered, this will put additional pressure on 2026/27 reserves and sustainability.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if the council is already off-track in the current year, and whether 2026/27 assumptions about reserve usage are realistic.
findings.figures: £5.1m overspend at Q2 2025/26. £3.2m planned draw from Voluntary Revenue Provision reserve for 2026/27. £6.0m drawn in 2025/26.
findings.quote: They also reflect that the Council is forecasting a £5.1m overspend for 2025/26 (at Quarter 2) and there are several pressures that are expected to continue into 2026/27 and in some cases beyond.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit growing to £78.5m despite Safety Valve intervention and growing faster than council's own contribution
findings.detail: The DSG deficit was £36m when the Safety Valve Agreement was signed in March 2022. The original timescale for elimination was 2026/27 but has been extended to 2029/30. Despite government contributions of £33.5m and the council's own contribution of £2.15m annually (with a further £2.15m in 2026/27), the deficit is forecast to reach £78.5m by end of 2025/26. This is driven by rising numbers, inflationary costs and case complexity that are outpacing funding. Although a statutory override separates this from the general fund, it remains a growing liability.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand if this council can manage a growing deficit in one of the most volatile budget areas. The trajectory is worsening despite intervention.
findings.figures: £36m at March 2022, forecast £78.5m at March 2026. Government contribution £33.5m total. Council contribution £2.15m annually to 2029/30. £14.7m overspend in 2025/26 alone.
findings.quote: There is a forecast overspend of £14.7m in year and increasing the deficit at the end of the 2025/26 to around £78.5m. This is primarily due to the rising numbers, inflationary costs and complexity of cases.

findings.headline: Strategic Budget Contingency of £3.5m is completely drawn down in the current year, leaving no buffer
findings.detail: The Strategic Budget Contingency reserve of £3,500k is fully deployed (estimated in-year movement of £3,500k) by 31 March 2026, leaving a zero balance. The glossary defines this contingency as held 'to fund budget pressures that may arise due to delays in implementing savings plans and/or issues that have arisen post the agreement of the budget.'
findings.matters: Complete depletion of contingency in the current financial year indicates the council has already committed all its emergency buffer to cover anticipated budget pressures, leaving no headroom for unforeseen issues or delays in delivering planned savings.
findings.figures: Strategic Budget Contingency (3,500)k revised April 2025; in-year movement (3,500)k; balance £0 by 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Strategic Budget Contingency (3,500) - (3,500) 3,500 - - - - - -

findings.headline: Voluntary Revenue Provision reserve grows from £11.3m to £50.2m by 2031, consuming much of the reserve growth
findings.detail: The VRP reserve increases by £4.8m in the 2025-26 budget (approved movements) and is projected to grow from £11.3m to £50.2m over the seven-year forecast. VRP funds voluntary overpayments of minimum revenue provision—in effect, pre-funding future debt repayment. This four-fold buildup represents the most material planned use of the council's reserve growth over the forecast period.
findings.matters: This material accumulation of debt-repayment reserves signals significant capital investment obligations or debt service scheduled ahead, and it reduces the council's liquid resources available for contingencies or other purposes.

These regulatory requirements are a major, non-discretionary driver of the £390m capital plan.
findings.matters: Regulatory non-compliance could trigger regulator enforcement and required remediation; compliance costs are material and unavoidable.

findings.headline: Council plans £390m capital spend after years of underspending, significant vacancies, and delivery failures
findings.detail: The paper acknowledges prior problems: 'lack of oversight, significant vacancies within the services, changing priorities for investment and lack of effective planning.' New staffing (£383k additional costs) and governance structures aim to fix delivery. Executing £78m/year average spend after recent failure is a notable execution risk.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver the capital program leaves compliance gaps and wastes borrowed money; successful execution is critical to the business plan.

findings.paper_title: HRA Rent, Service Charge Inflationary Uplift 5 Year Capital Plan Final
findings.headline: 51% of tenants in arrears; 73% benefit-dependent; 55% on Universal Credit which doesn't flow to council
findings.detail: The council identifies 'significant strategic and operational challenges' from welfare reform. Universal Credit is paid direct to tenants with a 5-week payment lag, not to the council. With 5,438 tenants receiving no benefits and over half the stock in arrears, income collection risk is material to HRA viability.
findings.matters: Income instability and collection delays threaten the HRA's ability to service new borrowing and fund planned capital works.
findings.figures: 51% of tenants in arrears; 73% on some benefit; 55% on UC; 5,438 tenants with no benefits; £200k allocated for UC transitional support
findings.quote: There are significant strategic and operational challenges in dealing with the claimants in receipt of benefits in Kirkle es Council tenancies and as UC continues to be rolled out in Kirklees, with increased risks associated with managing the HRA, cashflow and income collection rates.

findings.paper_title: HRA Rent, Service Charge Inflationary Uplift 5 Year Capital Plan Final
findings.headline: Capital plan more than doubled from 2024 estimate (£170m to £390m), requiring £186.3m of new borrowing
findings.detail: The March 2024 capital plan estimate of £170m has expanded to £390m to account for building cost inflation, new regulatory requirements (fire/building safety, Awaab's Law), and growth ambitions. This substantial increase requires £186.3m of new borrowing over 5 years—48% of total capital funding.
findings.matters: A material expansion of HRA debt requires confidence that income can service it and that capital spending will deliver intended outcomes.
findings.figures: £390m capital plan vs £170m 2024 estimate; £186.3m borrowing required (48% of total funding); £264m for home improvements, £105m for strategic priorities
findings.quote: In March 2024 we estimated that a capital plan budget of £170million would be required...However, that plan had not fully considered the extent of future building cost inflation and did not include other strategic Council's priorities

findings.headline: Property consolidation savings of £301k–£500k are still in planning stage and depend on completion of an external review before any closures occur.
findings.detail: Proposal PL2604 forecasts asset rationalization savings of £301k in 2026/27, growing to £500k by 2028/29. However, 2026/27 will be spent 'working with services and directorates to identify opportunities'; actual building closures and capital disposals are planned for Years 2 and 3. The document states this depends on 'information and data received following the external review', which appears not yet complete.
findings.matters: Large projected savings that remain in planning phase carry execution risk. If staff resist moves, disposals are delayed, or the external review identifies fewer rationalization opportunities than hoped, savings slip to later years or disappear, creating a funding gap.
findings.quote: Year 1 (2026/27) would be spent working with services and directorates to identify opportunities for rationalisation of assets / greater utilisation of buildings, with building closures occurring in Year 2 (2027/28) and Year 3 (2028/29).

findings.headline: The council is closing the Peripatetic Catering Service which operates at a £121k annual budget deficit due to declining school demand.
findings.detail: The Peripatetic Catering Service, which provides temporary catering cover to schools, has become unviable. It currently operates at a £121k annual deficit 'resulting from a decrease in schools purchasing this provision', and the council describes the service as 'increasingly challenging' in light of 'ongoing budget constraints'. Closure will save £61k.
findings.matters: A council cutting a loss-making service signals financial pressure. The broader signal is that school budgets are under strain—schools are buying less ancillary support from the council, which may indicate they too are in deficit.
findings.figures: £121,000 annual budget deficit; £61k saving in 2026/27 and 2027/28
findings.quote: Although it has contributed valuable operational continuity, sustaining the service has become increasingly challenging in light of ongoing budget constraints. Currently, the service operates with a £121,000 budget deficit resulting from a decrease in schools purchasing this provision.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care savings more than triple from £322k to £1.3m by 2028/29 by increasing assistive technology referrals, depending on successful adoption of a new platform.
findings.detail: Proposal AH2605 projects savings growing to £1.3m by year 3 by 'incrementally increasing referrals for Assistive Technology by 8 per month over 3 years'. This depends on successful procurement and November 2025 contract award for a new 'digital ARC (Alarm Receiving Centre) platform', and on service users and professionals actively adopting it. The underlying diagnostic was completed June 2025.
findings.matters: This is a large and rapidly growing saving that depends on successful technology implementation and user adoption—factors not entirely within the council's control. If adoption is slower than forecast, a £1m+ annual gap opens by 2028/29. Lenders need to judge whether this is strategic investment or optimistic forecasting.
findings.figures: £322k (2026/27), £906k (2027/28), £1,299k (2028/29); 8 per month referral increase over 3 years
findings.quote: Building on the diagnostic of the Assistive Technology offer in Kirklees completed in June, we will develop additional capability for Assistive Technology using the new digital ARC (Alarm Receiving Centre) platform which is currently being procured. The contract will be offered in November. Incrementally, we will increase referrals for Assistive Technology by 8 per month over 3 years.

findings.headline: 27 FTE staff posts are at risk of redundancy in 2026/27, requiring an HR1 declaration despite deletion of 28 vacant posts.
findings.detail: Total FTE reduction from all 2026/27 proposals is approximately 55, which the council is mitigating by deleting 28 currently vacant posts, leaving 27 posts at risk of redundancy. The council plans to make an HR1 declaration and may offer voluntary redundancy 'on a case-by-case basis' rather than council-wide. This is a material workforce reduction across multiple directorates.
findings.matters: Significant workforce reductions can affect service delivery quality, institutional knowledge, and staff morale, all of which matter to creditworthiness. Lenders want to know whether councils can maintain service standards and financial control during cost-cutting.
findings.figures: 55 total FTE reduction potential, 28 vacant posts deleted, 27 FTE at risk of redundancy
findings.quote: This means that the number of staff potentially at risk, because of the 2026/27 budget saving proposals, is currently 27. As such, we will be making an HR1 declaration of 27 FTE posts that are potentially at risk of redundancy.

findings.headline: The largest single saving (£1.45m) depends on reducing children in external residential placements, a demand-driven assumption.
findings.detail: Children's external residential placements savings of £1.45m in 2026/27 (declining to £735k by 2028/29) rely on reducing growth assumptions in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy. This is part of a 'sufficiency strategy' to move children to local, family-based settings. If demand for external placements does not fall as expected, this saving will not materialize and the council will face a funding gap.
findings.matters: This represents 21% of total new savings (£1.45m of £6.9m). Demand-dependent savings are inherently risky if the council cannot control the underlying demand drivers. A lender needs to understand whether this is a realistic assumption or optimistic forecasting.
findings.quote: This reduction aligns with our broader sufficiency strategy to ensure children and young people are supported in local, family-based, and regulated settings wherever possible, improving outcomes and reducing high-cost, out-of-area, or unregulated placements.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Mgt Mid Year Report 2025-26 CGAC FINAL
findings.headline: Internal borrowing (financing capital from reserves rather than external loans) has doubled year-on-year; forecast to reach £158.2 million by March 2026.
findings.detail: The council is accelerating reserve depletion to fund capital investment. Internal over-borrowing (the use of balance sheet resources to finance capital rather than external borrowing) was £74.8m in 2024/25 and is forecast to reach £158.2m by March 2026—more than doubling in one year. This increases reliance on reserves and will eventually exhaust them, forcing the council into external markets regardless of rate conditions.
findings.matters: Rapid reserve consumption reduces the council's buffer against spending volatility and provides less flexibility for managing cashflow; once reserves are depleted, the council loses its option to avoid unfavourable market conditions.
findings.figures: Internal over-borrowing 2024/25: £74.8m; forecast 2025/26: £158.2m; increase: £83.4m; total balance sheet resources declining from £133.4m to forecast £122.0m
findings.quote: The Council has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme and an estimated borrowing requirement as determined by the Liability Benchmark (see Appendix 4), which also considers usable reserves and working capital.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Mgt Mid Year Report 2025-26 CGAC FINAL
findings.headline: £30 million of LOBO loans are at material refinancing risk if lenders exercise call options; report identifies 'increased probability' given current high market rates.
findings.detail: Kirklees holds £30m of LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans where the lender can unilaterally propose a rate increase at set future dates. The council notes that 'with market rates remain high, there is an increased probability of call options on the LOBOs being exercised by lenders.' Although none were called in the first six months, 'there remains a possibility they could within the next 12 months.' If exercised, the council plans to refinance from other local authorities or PWLB rather than accept higher rates.
findings.matters: LOBO call risk forces unplanned refinancing at potentially higher rates in an uncertain market; £20.9m is at risk within 12 months, representing material near-term cost exposure the council does not control.
findings.figures: Total LOBO exposure: £30.0m; risk within 12 months: £20.9m; risk within 24 months: £10.0m
findings.quote: As market rates remain high, there is an increased probability of call options on the LOBOs being exercised by lenders. No LOBO loans were called during the 6 month period to September 2025, however there remains a possibility they could within the next 12 months

findings.paper_title: Treasury Mgt Mid Year Report 2025-26 CGAC FINAL
findings.headline: Council expects to borrow an additional £66.2 million for the year to fund capital programmes; Capital Financing Requirement is forecast at £1,012.7 million.
findings.detail: The council's underlying need to borrow for capital investment (CFR) is growing. The mid-year liability benchmark, based on updated capital plans, shows the council must raise an additional £66.2m of borrowing beyond existing levels to fund the capital programme for 2025/26. Total CFR is forecast at £1,012.7m, up from £939.3m actual in 2024/25.
findings.matters: Growing capital financing needs increase future revenue costs through asset depreciation, maintenance and replacement; lenders need assurance the council's revenue budget can sustain these long-term obligations.
findings.figures: CFR forecast 2025/26: £1,012.7m (2024/25 actual: £939.3m); additional borrowing expected: £66.2m; borrowing CFR: £930.1m
findings.quote: The mid -year forecasted liability ben chmark, based on updated capital plans, highlights that there is an expectation of additional borrowing of £66.2 million for the year.

findings.headline: Net borrowing increased £10.2 million in the first six months and is forecast to reach £808.1 million by year-end, up £92.7 million year-on-year.
findings.detail: The council's net borrowing position deteriorated from £715.4m at March 2025 to £725.6m by September. The full-year forecast is £808.1m—an increase of £92.7m on the prior year. Although this is lower than the January strategy estimate of £898.7m, the upward trend year-on-year reflects the capital programme and the council's growing debt burden.
findings.matters: Rising net borrowing increases future debt service costs and constrains the council's financial flexibility; lenders track annual debt growth as a key affordability metric.
findings.figures: Net borrowing March 2025: £715.4m; September 2025: £725.6m; forecast year-end 2025/26: £808.1m; year-on-year increase: £92.7m
